speechtext:
I would like to ask the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) whether it would not be possible for this House to have laid on the Table before we decide upon this question the documents which the government propose to execute as the agreement between the Dominion and this railway company. I think it is of the utmost importance to the country that before we enter into this guarantee we should have full knowledge what the terms of the bargain may be. It is quite obvious to anybody that the resolution laid before us gives most meagre par-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
ticulars of what is contemplated. The hon. gentleman assures us that rolling stock to the extent of $3,000 per mile shall be acquired by this company, and, I Piesumi. placed upon the railway and maintained there, and that the country shall have a first mortgage upon the rolling stock. l mention that here simply for the purpose of pointing out that no person would gather from this resolution that any such provision is intended to be put into the contract. The hon. minister tells us that it is the intention and no doubt it is the intention that this shall be done, but from the resolution that we have here, nobody would know that anything of the kind was contemplated. There is no word in this resolution about rolling stock. There is the one word 'property ' and everybody knows that no person taking a mortgage on a railway would consider that under the word ' property he had acquired rolling stock or any particulai amount of rolling stock. One car would cover the word 'property' if this one car were necessary to comply with the conditions of this resolution. Those who are at all familiar with the present methods or railway companies know that while tliej may have a large amount of rolling stock upon any given concern not one locomotive or car may be the property of the railway company. There may be a certain amount of rolling stock to begin with and within twelve months there may not be a car left.
I do not think it is right that we should be asked to pass a resolution committing this country to a very large guarantee without knowing really what we are doing. Me have to receive an assurance from the hon. minister that certain things that are proper and reasonable in such a transaction aie intended, but there is nothing in this resolution to indicate that they must be included in the terms of the contract. I do not suppose that the hon. minister has got to this stage of the transaction without having very carefullv considered and negotiated the whole of the'terms of this contract, and before we are asked to commit ourselves to a vote in favour of the transaction we ought to be as fully informed of it as the hon. minister is. Then, I would like to ask. supposing that this company goes into default, and the country is called upon to pay a large sum year after year upon the guai-antee, and we may be called upon to pay a million dollars in four or five years upon the guarantee, in what position do we stand in regard; to the indebtedness of the company to the country ? Are we to have interest upon our advances ? What are the terms in that respect ? If we pay $1 000,000 or $2,000,000 upon these bonds to the bondholders, is that to be a loan without interest, or has the company to pay us interest upon the advances ? Surely that is a matter in regard to which men looking after the interests of the country are entitled to know what the terms of the con-

tract are in that respect ; yet from the terms of this resolution they are completely in the dark. These are details, but most important details, and I do not think it is right that we should be asked to enter into a bargain of this kind and pledge the credit of the country to such a large extent without knowing more than the mere terms of this resolution.

I am unable to see that these resolutions are wanting in clearness in any respect, and I would not have supposed, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) had not assured the committee of the fact that they left one in any doubt as to the main principles involved in this proposition and that they did not as fully cover the ground as is necessary at this stage. I am not prepared to say, but that when the Bill is introduced it may not be found necessary to enter into fuller detail, but even if the Bill is in more detail it will be quite open for any member of the House who thinks that some conditions ought to be introduced, to move that they shall be included in the measure. These resolutions are simply introductory features so as to enable a Bill covering all proper and necessary ground to be laid before parliament. If when the Bill is introduced, the hon. gentleman has any views to suggest to the committee looking towards some additional clauses or amendments to clauses, it will be very proper for him to move them, and I am sure the committee will be disposed to give any suggestion of his the fullest consideration. The request that we should lay the contract on the Table, or the documents which it will be necessary to have executed after legislation is passed, is not a request that I am afraid I could accede to. We have not advanced to that stage and could not have advanced to that stage. The necessary drafting of the technical work which is required to be done by the Justice Department and the legal fraternity will be done when we have passed the Bill, and until the Bill is passed it will be inexpedient and I would submit to my hon. friend quite unnecessary for us to enter upon the drafting of the necessary agreements, contracts, and securities. Parliament is informed by these resolutions of the main conditions upon which we think that this guarantee could properly be given, and it must rest upon the responsibility of the government after the Bill has passed to see that the papers necessary to be executed between the parties are properly drawn. We will have to ask the House, as is customary in such cases, to treat us upon that basis. We have not the time to give to the necessary consideration to the working out these features. Having regard to the immense work which devolves upon us, we cannot expect the government to drop other necessary work and delay parliament while we are having 156$
these securities drawn up in technical legal shape and form.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister tells us that these resolutions contain all the information he is able to give us at this moment. He says we can obtain further information when the Bill is introduced; and almost in the same voice he tells us that the government will not be able to settle the terms of the contract until after the Bill has been passed.

I do not think the hon. gentleman would misquote me; but that is not just what I said. I said that when the Bill comes down, then, if my hon. friend thinks that there is not sufficient protection provided in the public interest, it is quite open to him to move any amendment he wishes to the Bill, and everything he suggests would receive a proper measure of consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I certainly understood the minister to say clearly, that it could not be expected that the government would settle the terms of these contracts until after the Bill was passed.
I said :	Would draft the contracts and have them drawn up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It will not be much satisfaction to this House and the country after we have passed the Bill, to know that the terms of the contracts are objectionable. It will be too late then. I do not see why in such a matter as this the House should not be placed as far as possible in possession of everything that is material to the consideration of whether we should give this guarantee or not. It is useless to say that negotiations have not been going on for some time with a view of the settlement of the terms of this guarantee. If it is not so, then the position we are in is this : that when the Bill is ^introduced the government will have no more knowledge than we have at the present time, and we will be asked to pass a Bill authorizing this guarantee and leaving it entirely to the minister to settle with the company what the terms and details shall be. I would like to call the minister's attention to the fact that when the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway was entered into it formed part of the Bill. It was a complete contract signed and sealed between Her Majesty and the railway company. It was introduced to this House, and parliament had the opportunity of seeing every word of that contract before they passed upon it.
Hear, hear.

Practically we are going it blind in this case, and I think it is most unfair to the House and to the country that we should be asked to vote on matters of this

importance when the minister tells us that after the Bill has passed the government will settle the terms of the contract. I would like now to refer to clause 7. It is a very simple clause which might have been introduced, not by the government but by the railway compnay. It is a way not unknown to introduce a clause that looks to he in favour of the country while it is really perhaps in favour of the company. It says :
Resolved, that the Governor in Council or any authority created by parliament for the purpose may also grant running powers over any portion of the lines hereby aided to any other line of railway upon terras considered equitable.
That is a very nice clause. Supposing that next year or three or four years hence, the government choose to grant running powers upon this line or upon some short distance of it to another railway upon terms that the government may consider equitable-why the terms the government may consider equitable may be the releasing of a large portion of the security that the country is now stipulating for. We are practically leaving the whole of this subject to be settled by Order in Council. I mention it as showing that it is of the utmost consequence to the interests of Canada that we should know every word and every detail of it before we commit ourselves to the guarantee. I am not endeavouring to obstruct the government in what they are proposing to do, but I do say tbat before we enter into an enormous contract of this kind we ought to know what we are contracting about.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) is indulging in very strong adjectives in connection with a proposition that certainly on the face of it does not warrant him in so doing. I surely do not understand my hon. frien<4 when he discovers anything like a reasonable analogy between the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway original contract and the Canadian Northern Railway guarantee. There is not to my mind the least similarity between the two. In the one case this country was giving without competition or tender, an immense amount of money, a large quantity of land, and other privileges, properties, and rights, of the most extensive character. We were giving all these things to the company, whereas this is an offer of the guarantee of the government, by way of security, to enable this company in the public market to raise money for the purpose of building the road, which guarantee is covered and secured by the property which is thereby created, and which every one believes will be well able to recoup the country for every farthing that is advanced or paid. If the hon. gentleman can discover any analogy between these two cases, be succeeds in doing what I think very few Mr. BARKER.
members of this committee will feel able to do. We afe providing here, I think in the amplest manner, that the property which is being created by the use of this guarantee, shall be subject to the liability to repay the loan contracted under the guarantee. I am not saying that these resolutions contain all that a Bill will contain or ought to contain. I have not yet got down to framing the Bill in its entirety, or dealing with it. When that comes before parliament, if it seems wanting in any respect, it will be quite open to parliament to make good any omission in it. The hon. gentleman refers to clause 7. That seems to me to be plain and clear. The hon. gentleman discovers under that clause a possibility of the government throwing away a large portion of its claim. My hon. friend might just as well say that we ought to introduce a provision in the Bill to say that the members of the government shall not steal the whole of the bonds, and dispose of them for their private advantage. What just reason or cause is there for assuming that under a clause which is manifestly a proper clause, providing for the granting of running rights, a government could absolutely wipe out the security that is given, or any part of it ? My hon. friend ought not, it seems to me, to discuss the resolutions from any such point of view. He is not approaching this question with the usual judgment that he applies to the matters which he considers. I would like to know what other language could be employed in clause 7. We cannot put in this resolution the terms it might be necessary to impose. What would be equitable terms must depend altogether upon the circumstances at the moment. What would be equitable under one set of conditions might be inadequate under another. Ought there not to be somebody vested with the authority to grant these running powers ? And if the Governor in Council ought not to be vested with that authority, who ought ? Is it necessary that we should wait until parliament meets before giving to any other company the right to run over the lines of this railway, and get the sanction of parliament to the express terms on which that right is granted ? That is not done in any ordinary case. At present the Railway Committee of the Privy Council has power to decide on what terms one railway shall have running powers over another. Why is it necessary in this case to introduce suspicions which do not attach to ordinary cases ? If this government is not entitled to the confidence of the House sufficiently to enable it to determine what are equitable terms, it is not entitled to the confidence of the House at all. My hon. friend, of course, has not any confidence in us ; but his suggestion, I apprehend, is not made from that point of view. He would, I suppose, make the same criticism and expect the same advantage to be taken, ev*n if his own friends were in power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Certainly. It is not the present government that is referred to here, but whatever government may be in power at the moment.

Then, whatever government commands the confidence of parliament must have that power. You cannot legislate in any other way. You must give somebody the authority to say what frill be equitable terms on which these rights may be exercised.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I suppose the minister would contend that it would be quite proper that the government of the day, whatever political party might be in power, could impair the terms of this guarantee in order to give running powers over this railway. That may be done under this clause.
I do not see it.

speechtext:
It is quite possible. The government of the day may determine the equitable terms under which another company shall have running powers. They may alter the whole conditions, reduce the rate of interest, or do anything else they like in consideration of the company conceding certain running powers. I say that any arrangement of this kind ought to be made with the approval of parliament ; and further than that, I say that the government of thp. (inv olinnM Iiotta-*

I do not say this with reference to the present government. I sincerely believe that this government is not going to be in power many years ; but whatever government is in power-when there is a Conservative government in power four or five years hence-it ought not to have the power to dicker with this railway company for running powTers on terms which would impair the security of the country. Suppose the country has to pay to bondholders .$1,000,000 in the next four or five years, what position do we stand in with reference to the interest on that advance ? There is not a word hinted at here with regard to that. It is simply an advance for the use and benefit of this company, without interest. so far as we know.

There is one point in this connection which I think has not yet been mentioned. This is not likely to be the last case in which we are to be asked for a guarantee ; and therefore it is reasonable to ask the minister to consider this case very seriously. Then, we must not forgot that these securities will go into the hands of investors, and then it will be too late for us to change the arrangement, because these
investors will have got vested rights which we shall have to respect. So far as this parliament is concerned, this is a new style of security. Ordinarily, I grant, the minister's position is sound-we adopt a resolution, and put the responsibility on the government of carrying it out. No one contends that all the details should be in this resolution. As an opposition, our duty is to assist the government as well as criticise, and in a matter of this importance, which, if reports be true, we will be asked to implement by still another transaction before this session is over, we cannot take too many precautions. We are assuming an obligation of $11,000,000.
A little over $9,000,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This resolution simply relegates the country to the position of a surety. If the surety pays a part of the debt, he is to that extent in the position of a bondholder. I do not think that the country ought to be satisfied with that. I think that the government ought to take some additional security, as for instance, a second mortgage from the company, and thus be empowered to act of their own violation and not have to go through the ordinary routine imposed on a bondholder. I think that, the bon. minister should endeavour to meet us half way and give us an opportunity to pass upon the contemplated contract before we are bound by it.

^STER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. There is no disposition on the part of myself or my colleagues not to profit by any suggestion which hon. gentlemen opposite may have to make, which would facilitate the carrying out of what we have in contemplation. But I do not feel free to give the committee any definite assurance that we will furnish the committee with the prepared documents-the mortgage and security and contract. In an important matter of this kind, it is very necessary that calm and careful thought be given to the working out of the proposition, and if we were to draft the documents "too hurriedly, there would be danger of error or oversight. I do not think that any interest will be served by hurrying this matter and adding it to the work at present before parliament. We lay down the conditions in our resolution, and in the Bill we will state any further conditions which we may think it well to submit to parliament, but we must ask parliament to allow us the time and opportunity to work them into shape in any agreement to be entered into between the company and the government. I do not think that it would be of advantage to the country and the undertaking, that we should depart from the rule in the present instance.
When was the rule laid down ?

If it was never laid down before, I am laying it down now. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is very much exercised concerning what would happen if the interest were not paid by the company and the government had to pay it. I would say to my hon. friend that the government would then be in a position to enforce the payment of that interest under its mortgage on the property. The government would be entitled to force a sale of the property or take it over. *
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you propose to collect interest on your advances ?

I will come to that in a moment. That is the power we would have ordinarily under these resolutions. Well, it is a question which the government must take into their serious consideration what would be equitable and fair treatment of a new enterprise and one which, admittedly, it is in the public interest to encourage, aid and promote in every way. Now, how should we treat a company having in hand a laudable enterprise of such great public interest and importance ? What would the people of Canada justify the government in doing with them ? Would they justify the government, in the initial stages of the enterprise, when the road is hardly in full operation, coming down and demanding the pound of flesh and telling the company they must forfeit their property unless they could pay the interest at once ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But you intend to . take the power to do that if you like ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the point.

There is no question about that. And the people who own this property and are making it subject to this mortgage realize that they will be in the hands of the government. Now, I am not going to suggest- nor do I believe-that the government would be warranted in pursuing their remedy in any other than a reasonable, moderate, thoughtful and deliberate way-give them time ; let them get their road in operation. We propose to have the right to know just what they are earning, how they are spending their money and what should properly come to the government from these proceeds. We propose to keep ourselves informed on these matters. We should deal- I am not now speaking for the government, for I know my colleagues have not considered this question-I am giving my individual, personal view, and I do not want to be understood as binding anybody else-we should deal with the company on the whole undertaking with a proper measure of consideration, after ascertaining what they have Mr. COCHRANE.
been able to do. If they have done all that they could reasonably be expected to do, the government should have leave to deal with them reasonably ; and I think parliament would sustain the government in dealing with them in a reasonable, lenient spirit.
Now, the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) is whether we should impose interest upon that interest. I have not considered it ; I do not know whether any of my colleagues have considered it. But I would remind my hon. friend that we are departing from a policy which has been followed ever since before he entered public life. Formerly money was given to the railway companies ; we have given away absolutely almost untold millions, and with the full approbation of my hon. friend. Now, when the government is starting out with the intention of adopting a new system as respects this undertaking, my hon. friend has discovered that there might possibly be interest paid by this government for a short period, and he would insist that we shall collect interest upon that interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He did not.
I merely wanted to know what the government intended to do about it. We want to know what the bargain is to be.

I am glad to know that my hon. friend does not insist, because it seems to me that, having regard to all that has taken place in years past, it would be unwise, in dealing with a meritorious railway that is being constructed for the benefit of the great country that we have in the west, an enterprise that is doing its best to realize the hopes and expectations of the people in every way, to treat them in a niggardly manner.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILAWYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to say that no one on this side of the House talks in any such strain.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILAWYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then, why does the hon. minister imagine that sort of thing ?
My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) would not do it, I know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Nor any other gentleman on this side.
I will acquit my hon. friend, and he ought to be satisfied with that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not want to be acquitted by the hon. minister ; I am not on trial before him. I would not like to depend upon his mercy, if he thought he could wipe me out. I do not see any reason for so much talk about this matter. The question was asked simply whether the government

intended to put themselves in a position to collect interest on the interest, if it were found necessary to do so.

I know that my hon. friend has a great aversion to talk. I hold his views and wishes in profound respect, and I do not wish to do any more talking than is necessary. Let me say, as he refuses to be acquitted, that I must convict him of wishing to treat this enterprise harshly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
No one on this side, I am sure, has any desire to obstruct the resolutions proposed By the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair). But I think we are bound to have reasonable information with regard to the bargain upon which we are about to enter. We are bound to know, in the first place, that the hon. minister who proposes the resolutions understands exactly the position he will occupy with regard to this railway company. It hardly seems to me, after following what the hon. gentleman said the other day, and endeavouring to follow what he said to-day, that the hon. minister himself has any clear conception of the bargain which he proposes that this country shall enter into with the railway company. The first essential is that the administration or department should know what they propose ; and the second essential is a consequence of the first-that when they know, they should make full disclosure to the House. Now, if hon. members of this House, having agreed to these resolutions, go to their constituents and are asked what is the bargain between the government and the railway company, I think there is not an hon. gentleman on either side of the House who would be able to tell definitely what the proposition was. It is not at all a question of confidence ; it is not a question of suspicion, as the hon. minister suggests ; it is a question of business principles to which we are directing the attention of the minister. It is a question whether the members of this House, they having but a delegated authority, shall further delegate that authority to the government, or shall determine the matter themselves as representatives of the people. Speaking for myself, I propose in every case, as far as I possibly can, to represent the people who sent me here, and to have a voice, so far as I can. in the affairs which concern them ; and not to delegate these matters to the decision of any other body. I believe it is the duty of this opposition, and it is the duty of hon. gentlemen who sit behind the ministry, to say that before we go any further we must know exactly what it is that is proposed. The hon. minister says : You must not have delay ; this will mean great delay, and the members of parliament, forsooth, will be sitting here idle until these documents are drawn up and laid upon the Table of the House. I propose nothing of the kind, Sir. I do not
propose, as a member of parliament, to sit idle and wait for this railway company, or any other railway company, to lay before this House the propositions they have to make in order to get assistance from this parliament. Whatever propositions they have to make should have been outlined in writing and should have been laid before the committee before now. So when you talk about delay, I say to the Minister of Railways that there should be no occasion for delay. These resolutions were introduced the other day, and it was then stated,
I understand, that the matter would be delayed for a few days in order that more information might be obtained. An hon. gentleman supporting the government suggested some of the information that we desired. None of that information is before the committee to-day. The Minister of Railways says that there is no similarity between the cases of the Canadian Pacific Railway and this railway. I admit that, to a large extent, he is right. In the one case we were supposed to be making a bargain by which we got in every instance dollar for dollar for our money ; and even then, when we were getting value for every dollar we invested, we had a bargain outlined and laid before parliament before we sanctioned the expenditure.
Did we get it V
Yes, my hon. friend got it. A member from the west should be the last man to raise the question whether we got value for building the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Oh, oh.

Yes, my hon. friend got value. A member from the west should be the last to assail the contract that made the west. A good many hon. members supporting the present government, a good many members of the government, too. do not like to be reminded of the value received from the Canadian Pacific Railway-men who condemned the Canadian Pacific Railway, and if allowed their way, would have prevented its construction. Not one of those members in parliament to-day from the west and supporting the administration, would be here to have a voice in the affairs of the country. We did get value in opening up that country- In the development of that country we got value over and over again for the investments made. But when I contrast that bargain with the proposition before us today-without saying that we should not perhaps aid this railway to some extent-and the minister saying that the two cases are not similar, I agree with him. In this case the railway company asks for a favour at tbe hands of the government, a favour which should be granted of course if it is in the interest of the country. But before we make that grant, it is the duty of members on both sides to see that it is a fair business

transaction, and safe in the interests of Canada.
Now, let me say with regard to the general question of assisting railways that I am unalterably opposed to giving money or lands for the purpose ; and when resolutions of this nature are brought before us, I regard it as my paramount duty to see that we are not giving the railway a subsidy under the guise of guaranteeing its bonds. I want to have the proposition so elear.y lfiid before parliament that we shall know that in no event will this country hereafter be called upon to expend money on this or on any other railway. If a proposition can be brought before parliament so clear, and definite, and so safe-guarded ' as that we can give assistance by way of a guarantee without it costing the people an expenditure of money, then I am willing to assist. But I want the Minister of Railways and Canals to make his bargain so clear that we shall not have to take anything on trust, I want him to outline a fair business transaction, so that we shall know that, in voting for the resolutions, we are not voting for anythng that will involve an expenditure later on.

I do not think there will be any disagreement with the Minister of Railways with reference to so fair a proposition as the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) made, and the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) fell in with, that when we have fixed by Act the terms of the guarantee and the security upon which that guarantee shall be held, it is only fair that the Bill should contain a clause that these securities shall not be impaired except by the same authority that created them, that is this parliament.
I do not think that the power to impair would be a safe power to place in the hands of the government. Perhaps it might be a safe power to place in the hands of this government, but some Tory government might follow, and then there would be trouble. I think therefore .that if we create these securities by Act of parliament, the proposition made by the member for Hamilton, namely, that they should not be impaired or lessened except by consent of parliament, is eminently fair, and I think the Minister of Railways as a lawyer would agree to that. But there are many more important questions even than that. It is clear that we are here entering upon a new policy with reference to the building of railways. So far as I am concerned, I have been for some time meditating the introduction of a resolution for the purpose of discussing the question of bonuses to railways, and I am prepared to take a position perhaps different from that which I see advocated in some quarters. The only question I am concerned about is whether the policy propounded in the resolutions is the wisest policy that can be

adopted. I undertake to say that when the Bill is brought down to parliament there are enough lawyers in this House to see that it contains every safeguard, both for the interest of the company and for the interest of the country. For I want to make a fail-bargain. I want the company that obtains our sanction to build a railway to have a fair mercantile chance to profit by it. I also want the interests of this country to be safeguarded, I want a fair and honourable bargain. I want it understood that in endorsing these resolutions we are not laying down a general statement of policy. In these resolutions, as I understand them, we are called upon to endorse a new policy, with reference to the building of railways, in general terms, but I am not bound to every proposition when the Bill is brought down. All I agree to is that if I vote for these resolutions I assent to the general lines of the policy, reserving to myself the right to object to every, de tail when we come to settle the clauses.
But, Mr. Chairman, there are many features that are far and away more important than the general question of whether we shall build railways by a direct gift of money or by a gift of land or by a guarantee of securities. The whole question of building railways in this country is one that we must discuss before the people. I undertake to say that the discussion that has been going on in some of the papers in Ontario for some time past completely misrepresents the public opinion of Canada. Why, some papers in Ontario say that the time has come when we should not bonus railways, when we should not lend the influence of the credit of Canada toward building railways. I say that doctrine is most narrow and unworthy of the people of Canada. We are just on the threshold of railway building in Canada. We have no railways in Canada. The country is almost as barren of them as it was upon the day when Jacques Cartier arrived, and I hope his spirit is not looking down upon the people of Canada to-day. I believe that if the French people had held Canada it would not have been so backward as it is to-day. There never was a greater heritage given to a people than that which has been given to the people of Canada and no people ever dealt with a great heritage in so unappreciative and miserable a manner as the people of Canada have done. I am bound to say that I think the people of Ontario are more responsible for the backward state of Canada than the people of any other province.
I say that kindly, because I am a true Canadian and I would vote for an improvement in the province of Ontario to-morrow with the sincerest friendship and with as much good-will as I would vote an improvement in the county of Colchester. But, I repeat, that the people of Ontario, have been a brake upon Canada, down to this time.

But, Sir, we will forgive the past. I believe that there is a uew breed of men growing up in the province of Ontario, who will help to carry Canada up to the great destiny which she should achieve in this century. I want the young men of this country to be impressed with the fact that we possess the better half of this continent. I am a geographical student of this country and if you give me twelve students, or twelve educated men accustomed to reasoning, accustomed to following the processes of logic to their conclusions, I will convince them from the physical geography of Canada that we possess the most dominant portion of the continent of America, and that if we play the game as men, we are destined to become the dominant, political and material power of this continent. We have a lot of men in this country who have been crippling public opinion, who have been crippling the ambition of the people, and I say that it is the duty of public men, instead of belittling the country, instead of crippling the great ambitions of the people, to stimulate them upon all occasions and to impress upon them that we possess the greater portion of the geographical surface of this continent, that we possess the greater lumbering interests, the greater water powers, the greater mineral resources of this continent and by far the greater agricultural resources and if we but be true to ourselves, we can in twenty-five years bid defiance to any power on this continent or anywhere else. But, in order to accomplish that high purpose we must plav the game of men and not the game of children. I said a minute ago that if Jacques Cartier came back here he would be ashamed of the progress that these six millions of people have made.

What about the hon. member for Jacques Cartier- (Mr. Monk) ?
Mr. GOURLEY'. And our friend Champlain. I am a great admirer of those magnificent French explorers who came out to this country, and I am certain that if power-had not passed away from them we would have been much farther ahead in the race of progress than we are. I have said that Jacques Cartier would be surprised if he came back here to find that we had not made more progress. And I say more ; if the great Indian chiefs came back they would not have much respect for the white men of this country. They would say : We had a pathway-of course it was only a pathway- from the great lakes down to Montreal and the maritime provinces along the shores! of the lakes and River St. Lawrence. What more have we to-day than a railway, a mere white man's pathway down the lakes and down the St. Lawrence ? The whole country beyond the mere border of the St. Lawrence and the great lakes is as sileut and undeveloped as it was at the time when
the Indian chiefs travelled those- pathways. They had also a pathway from the lakes down the Ottawa river. We have the same. We have the Canadian Pacific Railway stretching up through the country, but as far as any development is concerned the country is about in as undeveloped a state as it was when the Indian chiefs sang then-war songs on the banks of the Ottawa. Look at the great inland sea up there-Hudson's bay. That is one of the greatest seas in the world and if you will study the geography of this country and the situation of that sea, you will observe that it is in the centre of this continent. It was placed there to modify the climate of this continent, the climate is modified by it, and it makes the 60th parallel of latitude no colder than the 45th parallel which passes through the province of Nova Scotia.
Does the hon. gentleman mean Hudson's bay ?
Hudson's bay.

I thought the hon. gentleman meant a Canadian sea.
Mr. GOURLEY'. It is a Canadian sea four times as big as the Mediterranean. People in Europe talk about the Baltic sea. Why, you could take the Baltic sea and drop it into Hudson's bay, and it would scarcely cause a ripple on the surface. In regard to the Mediterranean sea. and we remember that the Latin and Greek books were filled w-ith references to this historic sea, this middle sea of the world, Hudson's bay would make four or five Mediterranean seas. If we play the game correctly, we will find that Hudson's bay will be one of the greatest seas of commerce of this continent. However, some persons may say, perhaps, that this is an unwarrantable prediction. I say no. To the student who sits down and studies the geography of this country, this is no exaggeration ; this is a fact. But we have to play the game. We must build railways in spite of what the papers of Ontario say. Who on earth edits the papers of Ontario ?
I never could find out. They say that we must stop building railways. I submit that, the necessity for building railways is now greater than ever it was before, if we are to take advantage of the enormous opportunities that are lying before us and everywhere around. We have a country which is far larger than the United States. We have 18,000 miles of railway, and the people on the other side of the line have 200,000 miles of railway. Divide 18,000 into 200,000 and you will find that it gives almost the exact proportion that 6.000.000 bears to 70,000,000. Just in proportion as the United States built railways they gained population and power. We have contented ourselves in this country with building 18.000 miles of railway. Having

18.000	miles of railway and 0,000,000 of people, we must adopt the logical conclusion that if we had 200,000 miles of railway, we would have 70,000,000 of people i'n this country. If we are to have thirty or forty millions of people in this country in the next twenty-five or thirty years, we must have 50,000 or 100,000 miles of railway constructed during that time. If we want to take our proper place in the march of progress, and challenge the admiration of the world, we must play the game and build
50.000	miles Of railway in the next ten years.
I will give the House an object lesson. The United States between 1860 and 1865 went through a great war. They had very few railways compared with their immense territory, and they met enormous difficulties and cost in moving their armies. When the war was over the public men said : We must girdle this country by railways if we hope ever to be able to dominate it as a political entity, and what happened ? From 1870 to 1880 in ten years, they built 60,000 miles of railway. Therefore, when I ask the people of Canada to stand up and be men and build 50,000 miles, I am not asking that which is unreasonable or has not already been accomplished under more adverse circumstances. I am a great imperialist and admirer of the English race, but I limit my admiration to the race of forty or fifty years ago. They went on and dominated the earth, but there was a little breed that grew up in' England forty-years ago that almost threw away the whole achievements of the Saxon race. That little breed known as ' Little Englanders,' I exclude from my admiration ; but fortunately. to-day there is a more dominant breed growing up ; owing to the genius of Joseph Chamberlain and two or three other leading men, who are again infusing into the people of England the ancient spirit that in the elder years conquered and dominated and civilized the earth. But while England hesitated a moment, during these forty or fifty years, they are girding themselves again for greater achievements, and now I hope some day to see the flag of England floating over the entire globe.

the public men of Canada in a great measure for that, because if the public men of this country' had gone upon the platform, pointing out that we had the best half of this continent, telling the people to stand by the flag and not cringe before the United States, we would have attracted a large share of that money, and in some measure won the attention of the world. If the United States in reply had attempted to take our territory we bad three or four millions of men tiiat could have beaten them back at any' time if we had had the men to lead and inspire them. But our leaders were craven, and if the leaders are craven the people will be craven. When Napoleon led the armies of France he chased the Germans and the Russians and the Austrians like sheep all over Europe. These same Germans who afterwards invaded Paris were scattered like autumn leaves by Napoleon, because Napoleon was a demi-god and he spoke to his men and he went up and down his lines before the battle and inspired Ins soldiers and they became demi-gods as well.

Splendid order. Mr. Chairman. That is the greatest compliment that could be paid me, because I have aroused the enthusiasm of the House. On one occasion Napoleon liad 60,000 Frenchmen whom he had deified by his own personality, and he said at ten in the morning :	' There are 150,000 Germans :
in the afternoon at six o'clock the whole lot of them were prisoners of war. But later on when France had no leader to inspire her people ; and when the Germans, Bismarck and YonMoltke, the whole circumstances changed. Therefore, I say that the people are just as big as their leaders, and the people of Canada unfortunately have not had national results in the true sense because they were without leaders who could arouse the national feeling of Canada. That has been the destruction of Canada. They had great leaders in the United States like Henry Clay and Daniel Webster who exalted the nation. I was out west one time in Illinois. It is a very level state, and has no hills higher than that table yonder. I was there on the 4tli of July and went to hear one of the 4th of July orators.
What did lie say ?

There was a little rise in the land, scarcely perceptible to a Nova Scotian, who is accustomed to beautiful hills and mountains, and that man described that hill as infinitely grander than the historic and renowned Alps, and the little brook 'that ran through his community rivalled in his mind the fabled Nile or the castellated Rhine. Sir, that is the teaching

that has helped the citizens of the United States to become great. Their leaders told them freely that they were the greatest people on earth and by and through the inspiration created by that teaching they achieved more than any other people, and 1 give them that credit, while detesting their very existence.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

Now, gentlemen, you must get away from all this narrow and provincial feeling and imitate the people of the United States in that respect. We must believe and declare that Canada is the greatest country on earth. '
Hear, hear.

We must recollect that by the new census-and that is the only thing we have to thank the Minister of Agriculture for-our territory according to the latest calculations of our geographical officers includes 3,745,574 square miles,while the United States, including Alaska, has
350,000	square miles less. We could put the United States into Canada and have a great province like Ontario and half of Quebec to spare. I was amazed the other day at the hon. member from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) underrating Canada ; if 1 had my way, a man like that would not sit in this parliament five minutes.
Hear, hear.

I believe that in a British parliament there is a constitutional rule that a member ought to defend the interests of the empire, and in this House there is an implied rule that every word that is said should be in the interest of Canada. Whef! a member violates that rule he should be at once promptly expelled from the House.
Hear, hear.

If we did that two or three times we would not have men getting up here to belittle Canada. The hon. member from North Norfolk said that Canada was an annex of the United States, and that Ontario belonged to the Mississippi valley and things of that kind. I expected to see a dozen men from Ontario resent the insult, but apparently they have become so accustomed to insult that they passed over the matter without the slightest protest. So far as I am concerned if a man maligns Canada in this House, I will get up and stop him if I have to act alone. If that had been done for the last thirty or forty years the right hon. knight from Oxford would have been stopped on many occasion.
Hear, hear.

There is a great national feeling growing up in Canada, that will not deal lightly with the public man who defames his country. We used to have
men in Nova Scotia who sometimes indulged in talk about annexation. They were few and far between and they never represented a particle of the sentiment of Nova Scotia, because the great body of our people were United Empire Loyalists, and we have no kindly recollections of the men who stripped our grandmothers and our grandfathers of every possession they bad and sent them down bare handed to the shores of Nova Scotia.
Oh.

We would be unworthy descendents of a great race, did we not resent such treatment, and if ever I were to say a word in praise of the United States, I should expect my ancestors to leap up from their graves to avenge me.
Hear, hear.

If that had always been the feeling in Canada, do you think we would be only 6,000,000 of people today. If we had had undaunted and dominant leaders, it would be to their eternal glory that Canada would now be far and beyond any other land on the face of God's earth. The public men of the United States were eternally vaunting their constitution ; this was a cruel misrepresentation, b'ut that did not deter them. In fact they have the most unworkable constitution on earth-a perfect jumble of tyrannies. If you asked me to say, what was the worst constitution in the world, I would say that it was either the tyranny of Algiers or the tyranny of the United States. An eminent man in the United States has recently declared that the constitution of that country is absolutely unworkable. It would have been found unworkable many years ago if any attention had been paid to it; but when the people were busily engaged in honest industry, they needed no government, for every man and woman governed themselves. But to-day, when they want a government, what have they got ? A Senate-a tyrant for six years; a House of Representatives- a tyrant for three years; a President-a tyrant for four years; and a Supreme Court, which bosses them all, eternally and for ever. The result is that a man who lives in the United States has four tyrants to deal with, whereas in Algiers you have only one, and if you get rid of him, you get rid of them all. Yet we had men in Canada willing to listen to these Yankees vaunting their constitution, when every man knows that the only constitution under which men are free to roam the world and win their way is the British constitution, and we have that constitution in the most perfect and refined form in Canada. Here the British race has the finest exemplification of British government in the whole world. We have improved on the English constitution as it is administered at the court of St. James. Yet for one hundred years we have permitted the

United States to claim that the only government on this continent, worth living under, is that of the stars and stripes. I am going to devote my time for the next few years to demonstrating that the only government that is worth living under is that of the old red-cross flag of England ; and I undertake to assert that the people of the United States will be the first to recognize the fact, because, having experienced the tyranny of their own government, they will be only too glad to get back under the old flag which they tossed aside 150 years ago, under the leadership of misguided and ruined men. If every man in Canada were inbued with a high natural spoix-it, in a short time this country would fill the eye of the world to the exclusion of the United States, and a vast population would be flowing into Canada. Then the building of 500 miles of railway would be the easiest task in the world. I desire to say to the people of Ontario that I hope they will stop talking about not subsidizing the building of railways. This is a new country, with only a few people in it. So far. the railways, are built only through those portions of the country that can yield them a revenue; they are built only along the rivers and in the settled portions of the country. The people of the United States felt that their country could not develop so long as its rear line was the Missouri river. They therefore said, we have to girdle this continent with railways, because otherwise we cannot expect to get population; and they built the railroads long before the population came. That is how the Englishmen lost their money. The railroads were built; the population did not come at once ; the railroads failed to pay in the first few years ; then the Goulds, the t anderbilts, and the Fisks got possession of these railroads, unforeclosure, and their fortunes were built up on that basis. What I am up for now, is to say to this government, and this parliament, that I am a railroad man ; I believe in the policy of building railroads rapidly, but what we want to do is to adapt the wisest method of accomplishing that purpose. The government must for many years be behind the railways. I am strongly in favour of the Trans-Canada; our railroads must be built much farther to the north; but how can we expect the capitalists to build these railroads without assistance from the government? Every one who studies the map of this country knows that neither the Grand Trunk nor the Canadian Pacific Railway can ever be of much value to us in the maritime provinces. They take the wheat from a country 500 or 600 miles to the north, carry it down to the lakes, and then proceed to carry it again to the north to Halifax or St. John, making the route a quarter longer than nature intended it to be. Therefore I am persuaded, from the study of the map, that these railways are Mr. GOURLEY.
too far south to yield us the greatest advantage due our geographical position. I do not say that they should not have been built. I admit that the southern routes were the only ones possible at the time. So eminent a man as Edward Blake, whom some on the other side of the House may still worship, though I think they are very foolish if they do, did Canada more injury than any other man of his time. He defamed Canada by endeavouring to make the people of England and the people of the United States believe, when the Canadian Pacific Railway was being built, that we had a country of no value. We had the greatest difficulty, when we were offering immense sums to induce capitalists to build that railway to get them to undertake it because gentlemen on the other side of the House did not give the government of that day, the fair play which I am giving to the government at the present time, and which I hope every Liberal Conservative will give them. They did not hold up the hands of Sir John Macdonald and Sir Charles Tupper, the two most distinguished men that God ever gave to this country.
Hear, hear.

God sent those men, as
he sent the great prophets of old to lead the people of this country to a high destiny. But when these men appeared, they were treated like John the Baptist in the wilderness, whom the priests and Rabbis went throughout the land and reviled and said, this man is preaching heresy, when in reality he was preaching those truths which, if they had accepted, would have given them eternal life. And if Sir Richard Cartwright and Edward Blake and the other men who led the Liberal party at that time, instead of imitating the Rabbis and the Jews, had aided Sir John Macdonald and Sir Charles Tupper to develop Canada, as I am now trying to aid this government to settle up on the best policy, they would have been more worthy of honour. I have not a word to say against this enterprise. I want to see the Canadian Northern completed and the Grand Trunk Pacific built. I want to see three or four transcontinental railways built in the next three or four years. The country is ripe for them; and if we play our game well, there will be plenty of business to make every one of these transcontinental lines a paying concern. With reference to guaranteeing the bonds of the railway, 1 am not so sure, whether that is the wisest policy on the part of Canada or not. I am not so sure that the best policy is not to give a lump sum to the railway company and be done with it. I am with the government with reference to giving no land. I think that is a wise policy. If the government would adopt the policy of giving every alternate block away for homestead purposes, but reserving every other block to reimburse the

government for the cost of building the railway, in the case of every transcontinental line, they would not only provide for every financial risk the government might assume, but would throw large sums of money into the treasury of this country.
Look at the lands which the Canadian Pacific Railway have sold, and you will find an answer to those timorous, faint-hearted creatures who figure out millions of loss with their little pencils and predict all sorts of blue ruin wherever any great enterprise is projected in the interests of Canada. The experience of the Canadian Pacific Railway has shown how unfounded are these predictions. What you require is faith and confidence, and you will find that there is nothing in the way of railway building which you can undertake which will not pay for itself in from five to fifteen years. Whatever assistance the government intends to give, let them give it in cash. In my opinion a cash bonus would be best in the interests of the country. We should not allow ourselves to be carried away by the idea that the giving of $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 is something tremendous. What we should consider is whether the building of the railway is fairly justified, and once we have decided that it is, let us not be niggardly in our assistance. We will perhaps be asked to bonus the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Well I have no objection to bonusing the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway. I want our country developed, and it will pay to develop it ; because until railways are built there are large sections which must remain unproductive. When the United States built their
60,000	miles of railway, the whole world rushed out to that country. Placards were posted all over England, telling the English people to go to the United States and there they would be paid from $2 to $4 per day. When these people went out to the new world, they found these enormous railways under construction. In ten years the American republic spent nine billion pounds sterling, or $45,000,000,000 on railway construction, which it filled the country with gold, and the Irishman who said that he could pick up sovereigns in the streets of New York was not so wide of the mark. For to be able to earn from $3 to $4 per day was tantamount to the mind of the Irish labourer to picking up gold in the streets. The United States played a winning game. They started every emigrant in the world writing:	' Go to the United States,' and they borrowed English money and fooled the Englishman and got their railways for nothing. But I want Canada to be honest, I want the men who put their money into railways in this country to get a fair reward. Circumstances are different in that part of our country, which has not yet been pierced by railways, from what they are elsewhere, and we therefore should I
be generous in our treatment of pioneer railway builders. And should we give them the assistance we ought, we will be amply repaid ten or fifteen years hence. From Ottawa to the Hudson's bay, the distance is in the vicinity of 500 miles, and there is scarcely a mile of railway built in that direction, and because of that lack of railway facilities, our country is sneered at as a little fringe of territory along the St. Lawrence and the lakes down to the maritime provinces. Had this transcontinental railway been built ten or twenty years ago, as it should have been, there would to-day be a different story to tell. A railway makes its own market. When you build a railway, you find towns and villages and settlements of all kinds, springing up, along its route, population flow-in, and the enterprise a paying undertaking in a short time. You give a new value to the land which repays a hundredfold the money expended in the undertaking. I am instructed to urge on behalf of the maritime provinces the building of the Trans-Canada Railway. From every board of trade, chamber of commerce and town council, resolutions have been sent me, as no doubt they have been sent to other hon. members, asking me to urge on parliament the building of this line. I hope that every hon. member from the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces, irrespective of party, will give his support to this project. Let us build thet Trans-Canada Railway and thus secure to Canadian ports the great traffic of the Northwest. By our present railway system, we are bound to lose a large share of that traffic. You bring the wheat down to the lakes, and you find the ports of Duluth and Buffalo waiting with hungry mouths to seize it, and once they can get hold of it, nobody else will have any show. If that is satisfactory to the people of Ontario, it is not to the people of the maritime provinces. We want the Trans-Canada, which will run away north four hundred miles, and from which branch lines will be built to those other lines running to the Great Lakes. The Trans-Canada will come out at the Saguenay river, just in the direction of England, whereas these other lines go to the lakes and there the trade is diverted to American ports. Having its outlet on the River St. Lawrence, the Trans-Canada will be directly on the line towards Halifax and St. John, or Country Harbour, which my hon. friend from Guysborough desires to see developed into a great port. If he succeeds in doing so, I shall not be envious. Wbat I desire is that the traffic should be brought to the maritime provinces, and then let the best port win, whether that be Halifax, St. John or Truro, or any other. If the government would propose a general measure of subsidizing all these transcontinental railways, that would be a policy which would appeal for my support. Instead of this being the

time to cease bonusing railways, it is tlie very time when we should begin. AVe should make it our policy to build 50,000 miles In the next ten years. If we should undertake this, money would come pouring in from all over the world, and it would then be said of us, as it has been said of the United States, that you could pick up sovereigns in the streets. The adjoining republic would send us in its people by the hundred thousands. I have heard it said that they would not make good loyal British subjects, but let me tell you, Sir, that any man who has lived in the states any length of time and then comes to Canada,' could not possibly be persuaded to go back, the contrast is too attractive. You could not drive him out of Canada with hounds. Such people would become the best citizens of this country, and these little Englishmen, on the other side, who are predicting the contrary, had better hold their peace until they learn something and form correct opinions of Canada.
With reference to this proposed guarantee of bonds, I would prefer, since the policy of giving land grants has been abandoned, giving a cash subsidy. I am not concerned about a subsidy of ten or twenty million dollars. I had rather give Mackenzie & Mann their subsidy in cash and be done with it. They are business men and would make the enterprise pay much better than if it were in the hands of the government. If the Canadian Pacific Railway had been dealt with as we are proposing to deal with the Canadian Northern, it would not have become the commercial success it is. If we were to adopt the policy of assisting railway construction by cash bonuses, the hon. Finance Minister would not object. Every year our revenue is leaping up by $8,000,000, $10,000,000 and $15,000,000, owing to the wise policy inaugurated by the late Sir John Macdonald. That great man built the Intercolonial Railway when we only had a revenue of $12,000,000, and the Canadian Pacific Railway when our revenue was but $22,000,000. Hon. gentlemen seem timid and afraid to build a transcontinental railway even at this late date. - Why, in a few years we will have a revenue of $100,000,000. When we built the Canadian Pacific Railway we had but a revenue of $22,000,000, and to-day we have a revenue of $65,000,000, which shows that the increase of our revenue is in direct ratio to the increase in our railway building. Let my hon. friend the Finance Minister set some of the calculators in his department at work, and he will find that there is a mathematical progression in our revenue, in direct proportion, to the increase in railway construction. It must be evident to any one who gives impartial study to the facts, that whatever progress we have made, is due to the wise policy of the late Sir John Macdonald and Sir Charles Tupper, who inaugurated the national policy
Mr. GO'JRLEY.
and the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was they who left us the magnificent heritage we enjoy to-day, and those hon. gentlemen who seek to have the credit of our present prosperity given to this government, remind me very much of the profligate and reckless heir who, having inherited a noble estate built up by a long line of virtuous and distinguished ancesters, would point to their pictures on the wall, and say : ' These are not the men who built up this heritage.' These fellows had nothing to do with it ; I am the one who alone made this magnificent heritage, and to me the whole credit is due.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we should have a general policy of railway building in this country. This is a new question, and I want the government to consider it. 1 was surprised when the hon. Minister of Railways, who is usually very logical, spoke so jauntily about adopting this new policy of his. He says that in former days we gave away millions to the railway companies, and that we should have taken mortgages on the railways for these millions. But, suppose such a mortgage had been proposed at the time when the m'oney was voted for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the opponents of the project would have said that it was bad enough to give away our millions, but that to take over such a mortgage would be eternal damnation. I am sure that Mr. Blake would have taken that view. And Sir Richard Cartwright, whose luminous mind I respect, when he devotes it to proper subjects of discussion, if it had been proposed to take a mortgage on the Canadian Pacific Railway for the twenty-five millions that was given them. I am persuaded would have wiped the dust of Canada from his feet for ever ; for he would have felt that Canada had better have been swallowed up in the waters under the earth. I say I am surprised that the hon. Minister of Railways treats his new policy in such a jaunty fashion. I am not certain but that the best policy is to make a lump sum of it, pay it out and be done with it-no mortgages, no securities, but let them go their way for "the guarantee may involve us in untold financial difficulties later. Take a good contract, a carefully drawn contract like that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and build the road, reserving the land. If this is done, I will undertake to say that in five years after the railway is completed, we shall sell enough land to pay the subsidy twice over and have millions of people coming into that country whose contributions will swell our national revenue and enable my hon. friend the Finance Minister, to come down in a few years -if he should be alive and well at that time-and announce that we have a surplus of forty or fifty millions for the year. If the government will subsidize the Trans-Canada, we in the maritime provinces will

feel that we are in a position to wish Mac-Ivenzie & Mann, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific God speed on their way.
I am for railways all over Canada. This is an imperial railway. With the Trans-Canada built, should we have a conflict for our territory, we would be able to maintain uninterrupted communication from end to end of our country, far from the border of the United States. I was speaking the other day with an eminent military man, and we were examining the map which the government has recently published. In passing I wish to thank those who have made that map. It is one of the greatest gifts to Canada. It lays our great country before us. Nobody knew what Canada . looked like until they had an opportunity to inspect this splendid-map. And I want the government to let me send thirty or forty copies of that map to the schools in Colchester, for it is. an education in itself. A copy of that map should be sent to every public school in Canada. It is the first map that has ever exhibited to us in its true light this enormous country of Canada. Why, my little boy when we looked at it, said : Pap, the United States are gone ; we are sitting on top of them. Well, that military officer said:	' Give me the trans-Canada
fully equipped and I will guarantee the safety of Canada. Let us build the trans-Canada five hundred miles away from the United States border, so that the British fleet on the Pacific and the British fleet on the St. Lawrence can give us supplies, and send them along that railway. Then, I care not if there were two millions of men against us, the campaign could be only a summer campaign, and we could retreat and retreat and play upon the invader the game that the Russians played upon the astute Napoleon. We could retreat-
Never.
Yes, the Boers have taught us that retreat is very often the prelude of victory.
Never retreat.

But, in the end, gentlemen, the snows of winter coming on, the invaders would be compelled to retreat. So,
from a maritime province point of view, that railway should be built, and built at once. Then from the general point of view, we should have a country opened up, five hundred miles in breadth, extending three thousand five hundred miles across the continent. The people would come in to possess the land and this country would spring from six millions of people to fifteen or twenty millions within ten or fifteen years.
If these railways now before parliament are to be subsidized, I urge, as a complement to these undertakings the subsidizing of the Trans-Canada. I speak in the interest of all Canada, for every one who knows me will acquit me of advancing any sectional interests or opinion. I would build a railway in British Columbia as soon as I would build one in the county of Colchester. I tell my people so when I address them. But the people of Ontario and flie people of British Columbia must be equally broad, and must agree to the building of the Trans-Canada, which will be the salvation of the maritime provinces. We can never have a great country unless we can bring our own products to our own ports to be shipped thence to the markets of the world. Is it not a disgrace to us that we have a trans-continental line which is building up Portland ? Every man in this parliament ought to be indicted for allowing such a state of affairs. If we had a proper national spirit in this country not one of us would escape punishment. To think of it-permitting a trans-continental railway that we have subsidized with enormous sums (for a great deal of the debt with which Ontario came into confederation represented money paid to the Grand Trunk, and we are bearing that burden to-day, but I do not complain of that)-permitting this transcontinental railway to build up a foreign port. I say we should give the Grand Trunk two or three years' notice to quit Portland. I do not want to do anything wrong or unfair. Vested rights must be respected, but we should not pay more respect to vested rights than we pay to the national rights of Canada. We should give the Grand Trunk three years' notice that they must leave Portland and establish their Atlantic terminals in Canada. If they could not sell out then-wharfs and other property except at a loss, let us compensate them ; for God's sake, get rid of the disgrace of a trans-continental railway of ours being permitted to build up a foreign port. I am amazed that this has not been debated in every hamlet in the country. But the people begin to understand. When I was at home not long ago. I was met on the street by Liberals and Tories alike who told me : Go back to Ottawa, for Heaven's sake, and put a stop to the Grand Trunk using Portland for ttteir terminus. That is the universal cry there.

I desire to say that I hope a Canadian will be appointed that will die in the ditches, that will die in the trenches, before surrendering the rights of Canada ; and if Canada sacrifices this territory, God heip the government that permits the sacrifice, because we know our rights in Canada at the present time. Now, Sir, I have done. I wanted to say many other things. There is a subject I desire to introduce in a day or two with reference to building a few railways in the county of Colchester. I congratulate the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) on the able and eloquent speech that he has given to us this dav. I regret exceedingly that he has been rubbing into his friends on his own side of the Mr. GOURLEY.
House their ignorance and their narrowness. I do not see why the young men of Colchester should want any maps to be sent to them, because I think they must be as enlightened already as his friends from Ontario on both sides of the House. Now, I think that Canada has made some progress, the province of Nova Scotia has made some progress. Time was when immigrants to Pictou had to come to Truro and carry their burdens on their backs when they wanted to put their seed into the ground. What do we see to-day ? Two pullman cars backwards and forwards every day from Halifax to Sydney, and a railroad to Windsor. There is scarcely an hour in the day or night but there is a train coming in or going out of Truro. The people of Nova Scotia built the road to Truro and Pictou before Sir John A. Macdonald had anything to do with the government of Nova Scotia. He says Sir John A. Macdonald was a great man. I do not want him to detract from the great men we have had in Nova Scotia, greater than any others that ever existed in the Dominion of Canada

Mr. GOURLEY'. I did not intend to.

And they will be remembered by their writings and everything else when very little will be said about Sir John A. Macdonald, or Sir Charles Tupper either. Now, the hon. gentleman can go from Truro to Halifax in a pullman car, he can get his dinner in a dining car, ns fine a meal as he would in any hotel in Montreal. I do not thinly it is well to speak slightingly of the progress that has been made in the Dominion of Canada. I have lived long enough to admire the progress made in Canada, both in railways and canals, and I hope that progress will be continued in future-not by leaps and bounds, but gradually, wisely, little by little. That Is the way to grow, that is the way the most permanent progress will be made. When I was listening to the hon. gentleman, to his most eloquent speech, that has created the greatest sensation of any speech that I have heard in this House, and I have been a long time in it, 1 was thinking that our hon. friends opposite made a great mistake in the selection of their leader, that they ought to have selected the hon. member for Colchester as their leader-

I do not see in the ' Hansard ' that the Minister of Railways stated whether it was the intention of the government to assist this railway as a transcontinental line, or whether they intended to continue this line from Edmonton to the coast. Prince Albert ought to be very well satisfied with the generosity of this and other governments in having three roads run to that particular place. I do not know whether the hon. minister explained the particular reasons that influenced the government in regard to the building of that particular branch, and I would like the hon. minister to state when the Bill comes down, the policy of the government in reference to this particular road as a whole. Surely the hon. minister does not intend to assist this company in building a road from Gilbert Plains to Edmonton unless he contemplates this being a transcontinental road. Surely the committee is entitled to a statement showing what the security will amount to. I notice, although it may be supplemented afterwards in the Bill, that the resolution does not propose to give any security on the rolling stock at all. It would be impossible to give any security on the road as already completed, because the company do not own the rolling stock. If I understand correctly the rolling stock belongs to another company which has loaned



it to the Canadian Northern and which receives a rental for the nse of it. I notice that the resolution carefully guards against any promise of giving any security upon that, showing that it has evidently, passed through the hands of the company's solicitor. I notice that there is no provision to meet the case of a default in payment. There is no provision, if there is a default in any of the payments against the whole of the amount of money becoming due. I think we should carefully guard against such a contingency. I remember a case of a railway in Nova Scotia which had received assistance from the government down there, in which it was maintained that default in the payment of any portion of the interest or principal did not deprive the railway company of its franchise or right of running the road until the whole of the aid had been given. There is a new phase in which it is said ' the government shall be subrogated in all the rights of the holders of the securities.' My hon. friend has in his mind the idea that there will no doubt be chartered during the present session a railway called the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I apprehend that he is somewhat curious to know why we do not mention that road in this resolution. In the first place, there is no Grand Trunk Pacific actually there; there may never be. But my hon. friend will say that it could be as well stated that this railway should not connect with any other main line. This will be, I think, a very great and very important line. We hear a good

deal and see in the newspapers a good deal about ah amalgamation or purchase of the Canadian Northern line by the Grand Trunk Pacific. Supposing that should take place, it would not, I think, be very prejudicial to the public interest-I am speaking my own view; but I think it would be a very serious thing if, by any combination which could be made, it became permissive to the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific to amalgamate and become one line. We know that the tendency of these great through lines is to acquire every other line within possible reaching distance. The tendency is to absorb everything in sight; so that if you have two competing powerful transcontinental'lines, you guarantee to the people a measure of competition, and give them an additional security which would be wanting if there was a combination of all the lines.
