I would like to ask the minister if that is not a new departure.

I hope my hon. friend will acquit me of any intention to be discourteous to him if I laughed,* because it was far from my intention. 1 laughed simply because of the fiery way in which my hon. friend objected to the answer given, which was not accepted by an hon. gentleman on the other side. The question was asked by the hon. member for Marquette why provision had been taken in this Bill to prevent the amalgamation of the Canadian Northern with the Canadian Pacific, and why a similar provision had not been made with regard to the projected Grand Trunk Pacific. The reason has been given by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. I am simply repeating the idea already conveyed to the committee. The Canadian Pacific Railway is already an entity; it is built and in operation. It must be evident that if the Canadian Northern Railway were to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the two were to come under the same management, the people of the North-west would lose the benefit of the competition, and therefore we insert this provision to prevent such an amalgamation. I do not understand that the wisdom of this provision is challenged by anybody opposite. I think my hon. friend admits its desirability, but he asks why a similar provision is not made with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ? For this reason, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is not an entity, it is a mere project in the air, which may or may not take place. What is important is that a rail-

way should be built, not only in that section of the country which this subsidy would cover, the valley of the Saskatchewan, but also that it should extend southward and eastward towards the tidal water. Then it is a matter of no consequence whether we have an extension to the sea by the Grand Trunk Railway alone as well as the existing line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or by an amalgamation of the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway. It is only one railway which it is contemplated to subsidize-if it is to be subsidized-and one line to be put in operation. The two cases therefore cannot be put in the same category. In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the wisdom of the provision is obvious, but there is no reason to apply the same treatment to the other projected railway which goes by the name of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems to me that the announcement made by the hon. the Minister of Railways and the right hon. the Prime Minister is of the utmost possible importance. It seems remarkable that this announcement should have been made only incidentaly after two days discussion. Here is a clause providing that this railway shall not amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways, in very vague terms, attempted to draw some distinction between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and the reason he gave, which has just been repeated by the right hon. gentleman, is that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is not an entity at xiresent, and we need not guard against it. But it will be an entity very soon, and it is obvious that some similar provision must be made either in this or in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway charter. My right hon. friend shakes his head. I would like to understand 1f it is undesirable to amalgamate the Canadian Northern Railway, with the Canadian Pacific Railway, what reason does my hon. friend give for amalgamating it with the Grand Trunk Railway or how in the public interest can it be right to amalgamate it with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The reason he Jias suggested is that that there is no entity to provide against and the danger is not existent. But if the intention of the promoter be carried out and if the intention of the government be proceeded with, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be an entity and the danger which these hon. gentlemen say will be caused by an amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific Railway will exist equally in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, except for another important announcement which the Minister of Railways made, and rvhicli is practically this, that the line which we are asked to subsidize

I made no announcement.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax) -is to be the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. If the hon. Minister of Railways did not make that announcement, I do not understand the English language. He made it as distinctly as he could. He said that there rvas no doubt that if this project went on, it would be the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway for a transcontinental line. Minister of Railways said the other day stood alone by itself, which we are not to deal with in connection with a transcontinental line, and yet the intention in the mind of the hon. Minister of Railways and the government is that we are really doing this as part of a proposed transcontinental line, the charter for which is going through the House at present.

speechtext:
I said nothing to warrant such a statement. What I did say was that I had seen in the newspaper press-as other hon. gentlemen have, no doubt-that there was some talk of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway coming to an understanding and combining their interests. That is a matter of common rumour, and I can only say that I am in no position to make any announcement that anything of the kind is either probable or possible, nor did I do so. If we were to express an opinion, I would say that it is neither possible nor probable, but it is stated in the press, and I was giving that rumour by way of explanation to show hon. gentlemen how impossible it would be, if a thing of that kind were to occur, for us to insist that it should not take place. I think it would be an eminently proper thing to happen, but it is not likely to happen and I did not announce that it was going to happen.

About.eighteen months ago, we discovered a conspiracy which had its origin in Skagway-perhaps it was not serious, or it may have been serious ; at all events it existed-the outcome of which it was said, would be an attempt on the part of American desperados to take the country. The whole territory is patrolled at present and we have the 300 men distributed at thirty-five different posts. Last year and the year before there was a great deal of small-pox all over the continent. I am happy to say that the Dominion of Canada has apparently been free from it for some time, but in the United States there has been a good deal of this disease and requests have been made from the local authorities, municipalities and others, that we should guard the frontier against incursions of small-pox. Are there any stationed at Sarnia or Windsor ?

No. We were informed that Detroit is
very well organized to combat the disease and there being no danger, there was no necessity for an appointment.
How do these officers perform their duties ?
They meet the trains generally on the American side and board the train and examine the passengers as they are coming into Canada. If they find a diseased person they stop him.
Do they report to the department yearly or half yearly ?
They give monthly reports.
How many cases did they detect last year ?
I am informed that they have not actually found a single case. The fact that they were there, prevented anybody having the disease from coming in.

I personally attended one man that came across the line last winter who had it when he crossed the line. To say that diseased persons are prevented from coming in is to say what is not a fact. I am told that the work is performed so perfunctorily that dozens of cases might come across without ever being detected.

We have had one or two cases reported to us as having come across the line. In some cases the municipalities have made a demand upon us, but when most of these cases were investigated it was found that the persons did not cross the line having the disease. I wonder that the case mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) was not brought to my attention.
The man came from Dakota, and I attended him myself and he told me he had the disease crossing the line and that it was apparent then as it was when I saw him.
At what point did he enter Canada ?
I do not know that.

We do not have officers on every railway that enters Canada. We get reports from the United States officials as to the amount of small-pox in the different states and whether it is active or whether it has decreased. If in the judgment of the superintendent general of public health there is no danger there is no appointment made. If the local health officer or other local officers represent that there is danger and if their demand is founded on reason we make an appointment. The case mentioned by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) may have come across where there was no officer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who made the demand for a medical officer at Bruce Mines and what railway comes in there ?

There is no railway hut there are ships coming across the lake. I am informed that there is considerable traffic from Michigan to that port and that there is small-pox in the Michigan lumber camps. Dr. Parker was appointed at $100 per month.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why is it necessary to have an officer at Thessalon ?
For very much the same reason as at Bruce .Mines.

We have the statement from the minister that no cases of small-pox have ..been detected by these officers. Those who live at places where these doctors are appointed look upon it more as being a political job than as being of any public utility. We have a large amount of money paid out to these officers who have not detected a single case of the disease and it seems to me that it is high time that these appointments should be cancelled.
The disease has been imported several times without detection.

The doctor who formerly acted in the Owen Sound district, has left there during the past year, and the department has appointed Dr. Hershey. I wish to ask the minister on whose recommendation Dr. Hershey was appointed ? I know that a great deal of dissatisfaction exists owing to the fact that medical men who have had a great experience and who have been in the town for years have been overlooked, while a man who is practically a new comer has been appointed over their heads. A great deal of dissatisfaction exists, and there is no necessity for this official. I would like the minister to say who it was recommended Dr. Hershey for this position in Owen Sound?

I cannot say on whose recommendation Dr. Hershey was appointed. His predecessor was appointed on the recommendation of the late Dr. Horsey, but he went away not very long ago. I take for granted that Dr. Hershey was recommended by the Liberal candidate in the last election, or by some other leading Liberal in the constituency.
Then I understand that the appointment was made on the recommendation of the Liberal candidate in the late by-election ?

I am informed that this appointment was made while the minister was away, and while I was acting for him. In that case, I am Hon. Mr. FISHER.
responsible for the appointment. I have no doubt I obtained the recommendation from one of my colleagues from Ontario in the administration, and 1 have no doubt that he received it in the way the hon. gentleman suggests. That is the usual way.
I would like to know how these officers are paid ?
One hundred dollars a month for the time their services are required.

As you have not succeeded in detecting one case of contagious disease through these officials, what is the necessity of continuing the service ? It is not popular in the country and why the government should insist on making these appointments when no service is given to the people is more than I can understand.

The work connected with the quarantine is all preventive. I appreciate fully what the hon. gentleman says about the people not appreciating the necessity of the service so long as no glaring case occurs ; but every now and then there is a case of disease entering the country and loss of life occurring, and a large expenditure of money being required to combat the disease. The whole quarantine system is for the purpose of preventing that, and if it succeeds in doing so, there is nothing to show actually the effect of the work except that there is the negative advantage of disease not coming into the country. We might dispense with the service in a certain county to-morrow, and in a few weeks we might have a case of disease entering that county. On the other hand, we might continue the service for a year and have no case of disease coming in. But the quarantine system is acknowledged in the country, it has been in existence for many years, and the people have demanded over and over again that they be protected from the incursion of disease. I may say that before this system of quarantine against the incursions of small-pox from the United States was adopted, there were representations by the dozen from the municipalities and individuals, protesting against the exposure of certain localities to that incursion of infectious diseases from the United States. It was in consequence of these representations that the system was adopted, and it has been carried on in the same way ever since. It is well understood by the local health authorities that we are doing this work, and occasionally representations come to us from particular places, setting forth their danger and requesting us to make an appointment. As a rule, our officers examine the condition of affairs, and if there appears to be danger, the representations of the local authorities are carried out.

Tlie lion, minister says tliat if the disease is found on the American side, an officer is always appointed to prevent it coming in. I am credibly informed that a case of small-pox came into Collingwood from Dakota, where the disease had been in existence for a year or two back. Another case came from Wisconsin. At different times different cases have been brought over in the last few years to my certain knowledge, and not a single one has been detected by these medical health officers. It seems to me that though they are appointed to receive a salary, they do not do the work very effectively, or these cases would not be imported. X could understand a case not being detected when the disease has not developed ; but in these cases the disease was developed when the men crossed the line, and was as apparent then as it was afterwards when it was brought to the attention of the medical men ; and yet they passed in without any interference whatever.

The hon. gentleman says he knows these cases of his own knowledge, and I accept his statement. Then that individual must have passed through a place where there was no physician watching the trains. I cannot believe that if one of these physicians was watching the train, a case of that kind could pass without detection. I stated a few minutes ago that the provincial health authorities in many instances made demands for this protection. I have just been informed that within the past two weeks we have had urgent representations from the provincial'health authorities of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, that we should not cease this protection on the frontier against infectious diseases coming in from the United States, and I may say that only to-day a statement was made to me that in the state of Montana, south of the boundary line of Alberta, there is a great deal of this perambulatory small-pox going about.
Does the officer at Colling wood board every boat that comes in V
It happens that we have no officer at Collingwood.

I may say that the service of these officers at lake ports is not at all satisfactory. Boats come in like the Canadian Pacific Railway liners, carrying 200 or 300 passengers. The doctor may be at his practice or anywhere else when a boat comes in, and by the time he reaches the wharf, if he reaches it at all. a great many of the passengers have left.
I do not think there is a satisfactory inspection. We have not been free from smallpox in Owen Sound, and yet not a single case of infectious disease has been detected by these officers. As nothing has been done
by them, I think it would be well to dispense with their services. I do not think this service is of any advantage to the town of Owen Sound, and the present appointment is very unpopular.

I will certainly try to find out, and if the provincial health authorities and the local health authorities consider it quite safe to dispense with the service in Owen Sound, I will be happy to do so. I have given strict instructions that whenever possible the services of any of these physicians should be immediately dispensed with. In reply to the hon. member for East Grey, the duty of these physicians is to board every train and boat and examine the passengers. If a passenger comes from what is called an infected district in the United States, and has not been recently vaccinated, it is the duty of the physician to vaccinate him. If a passenger does not come from an infected district and shows no signs of the disease, he is allowed to pass, but if he shows any sign he is detained.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is there an officer at Niagara ?
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why ?
Because in New York state and Buffalo and that neighbourhood, there is a very thoroughly organized system of combating the disease and keeping it under control.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why has the hon. gentleman an officer at Chippewa, a few miles above Niagara Falls, where they cross in row boats ? It is evident that physicians are only employed who have political pull. At Kingston, Gananoque, Brockville, and Prescott, whicli have a ferry service, there,are no officers, but at Chippewa, and Cornwall, where the people cross in boats, there are officers. At important points such as Niagara Falls and Kingston, where we have railways and ferries crossing every hour of the day, there are no officers; but at Thessalon and Bruce Mines, Beaver Mills, Cedar Springs and other places, where there is practically no traffic, we find an officer.

In the state of New York there is a very efficient health organization which looks after the disease, but in Northern Michigan, from wljich point people come to Thessalon and Bruce mines, there is no such organization and a great deal of disease, and consequently much more danger of its being carried to Cana da from there than from New York. At Chippewa there was an officer a very short time in consequence of the fact that there was an outbreak of small-pox in Buffalo or somewhere in that neighbourhood, which occasioned momentary alarm.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: At Chippewa, Mr. Grey drew a salary of $493.35 last year.

Where a physician is engaged permanently by the year, is he allowed to continue in general practice'?
I was surprised when the hon. member for Grey told us that this doctor was probably attending to his other practice. I remember when the Conservatives were in power, that there were strong arguments put up against Dr. Hickey practising in Morris-burgh while he was superintending tlie canal. He was compelled, owing to the opposition put up in the House by the opponents of the government, to discontinue his practice. I see that the doctor at Beaver Mills received twelve months salary and in addition he inspected four vessels for which he made an additional charge of $4 per vessel. If this gentleman was appointed permanently, I would like to know why he charges for inspecting these vessels ? Are these men who are thus bonused to be allowed to practice in opposition to other physicians in the same town. Where is Beaver Mills ?
Somewhere in the neighbourhood of Rainy river. I do not know how this doctor came to charge a fee.

On page D-97 of the Auditor General's Report, Doctor A. A. MeCrimmon is down for salary from May 30th, 1901, to .Tune 30th, 1902, at $100-$1,-306.45 ; inspecting four vessels at $4 ; vaccine tubes, 300 at six cents-$1,340.45.

I cannot explain the fee. He had no right to charge any fee, if he worked at $100 per month. The hon. gentleman asked if these physicians are allowed to practice. They are, provided they do the work which they are instructed to do, namely, meet every train and boat and examine the passengers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where is Mine Centre located ?
It is fifty or sixty miles above Fort Francis on Rainy lake. Beaver Hill is near the mouth of the Rainy river where the Canadian Northern Railway crosses from Minnesota.
There is no post office there ?
Yes, the Rainy river post office.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who is the doctor at Mine Centre 1 There is a Mine Centre on the Canadian Pacific Railway between the ' Soo ' and Sudbury.
I do not think that there is any station called Mine Centre on the Canadian Pacific Railway at all, certainly not between the Soo and Sudbury.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: Is there any regulation in the department which will cause these gentlemen to refrain from attending to their ordinary practice every day
No.
Will the hon. minister lay on the Table one of the monthly reports sent in by these officers ?
I can lay that on the Table another day.
Has not the hon. minister one of his reports now, with his officer there ? I am particular about one from Owen Sound.
No, I have not one at hand.

It does seem to me that this is almost a burlesque in quarantine. The minister says the medical man Is expected to attend every boat, but that he can continue his practice if he does that'! Suppose a medical mail is away in the country several miles distant attending to his practice. As often happens, he is detained away all day. The boats are coming in at the regular hours. How is it possible for him to attend these boats ? Or, say, he does attend the boats, what then ? Take the case of Owen Sound. The boat comes iu with perhaps three or four hundred passengers. If you stand beside the gangway you see these people coming off as quickly as they can rush. The medical officer does not board the vessel before it comes to the dock. The passengers may 'come from Sault Ste. Marie, or Port Arthur, or any of these other ports. So far as I know7, no examination is made of them and it would be impossible for a medical man to make even the most cursory examination of the passengers who get off these boats in the short time at his disposal. I can readily understand how cases come in w7itli smallpox actually developed on their persons and there is no knowledge of it until it comes under the attention of some medical man throughout the country. This has happened more than once, and more than twice, to my own knowledge within the last two years. And, I was going to say, that in every case they have passed where there was a medical quarantine officer standing. I do not know that I should be correct in saying that. But certainly there are cases in which the officers have allowed persons infected with small-pox to come in. The officers are paid so much salary, but I frankly confess that, in most cases, they do very little for it.
Mr. MeCREARY. So far as Manitoba is concerned, in my opinion, the men who are there looking after the quarantine earn their money and earn it w*ell. I believe that had it not been for the quarantine we have on the boundary there would have

been almost an epidemic of small-pox in Manitoba last year. As it is, a number of cases have come across. Some from Sprague, on the Canadian Northern, were held up in the cars at St. Boniface two days before they were taken to the quarantine hospital. Others come in by Gretna, Deloraine and Emerson. I believe that not only are these officials required, but extra officials are required along the boundary line. In fact, the officers could not do the work were it not for the assistance supplied by the mounted police. There is another point concerning which I desire information, either now or when the other items relating to the service are under discussion. In the Committee on Immigration the other day it came out that there had been brought into this country over 300 immigrants suffering from trachoma, and favus, two diseases that are considered contagious and dangerous by the American officials, so much so that the American officials refuse admission to immigrants infected with these diseases. It came out in the committee, in the minister's absence, that these people had passed the officials at Halifax and Quebec and gone on to Winnipeg, and from there had attempted to get into the United States. The United States officials, seeing the danger of immigrants coming through the port of Quebec and Halifax and getting into the United States across the northern boundary into Dakota, have stationed no less than fifteen officials, I believe, along the boundary line, to prevent immigrants from Canada going into the United States. As a consequence, in the month of April or March they deported or refused admission to about 380 people. These people were brought back to Winnipeg and are now in that city. I would like to know if the minister is going to bring down in his estimates an appropriation to look after these people infected with these contagious diseases. They are living in the north end of the citv, in crowded houses. I think it will be the duty of the minister to help the city of Winnipeg to look after these people, or else provide a train and deport them to Europe. The expense of caring for them or deporting them should not fall upon the city of Winnipeg.

I would like to point out that there is a difference between what are known as quarantinable diseases and other diseases commonly called contagious. The disease the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) men- ' tioned, trachoma, has not been held to be a quarantinable disease in any country where quarantine laws are in force. The stopping of these people from entering the United States is not affected by action of quarantine officers in that country, but by the action of the immigration officers. In the same way, in this country, at Halifax, St. John and other places, my colleague, ,the Minister of the Interior, directs a certain examination of immigrants from the immigration bureau standpoint. But that has nothing to do with the quarantine service, which defends the country from certain diseases called quarantinable diseases.
The quarantine department has nothing to do with immigrants coming in with trachoma ?

Every ship must be passed under examination by quarantine officers for quarantine diseases. Trachoma is not one ot these diseases. My officers in Quebec, St. John or Halifax would not stop any passenger who had trachoma. The immigration officers would stop an immigrant who had trachoma, but they would not stop a first-class passenger if that passenger happened to be suffering from the disease. Now, if people affected with this disease have come into Canada, that is something over which the quarantine department has no control. We have no power under our Act, no authority from parliament, to deal with these people. We could not seize them or stop them. But the immigration authorities, under an Act which was passed last session or the session before, has authority to stop them and deal with them. In reply to the observations of the hon. gentleman opposite,
I would point out that, in the United States, on the 1st of June, there were over 2fi,000 cases of small-pox, and of these no less than 19,000 were in cities contiguous to Canada. The North-west has been referred to. In Minnesota there were 3,553; in Wisconsin, 1,313; in Michigan, 633; in Ohio, 4,390. These figures show that, along the frontier of Manitoba and the lakes, there is a very great prevalence of this disease. I could at once dismiss all these officers and allow the passage of people freely across the boundary. But my department has received the most urgent aud persistent representations from the provincial health boards, the local municipal health boards and officers of various corporations along the frontier on this question. If I were to dismiss all these officers, I should raise a storm of indignation throughout the Dominion of which hon. members, I believe, have no conception, which no minister, government or parliament could ignore, and which they would hardly care to face. The people of the country are desirous of being protected from disease, they are anxious about it, nobody can blame them for it; and we have to take the steps that are necessary, in the opinion of the best medical authorities and the best health officials that we can find, to protect people from the incursion of disease. It is possible that we do not do enough, it is possible we might have an officer on every line of communication from the Atlantic to the Pacific which crosses the American boundary; it is possible we might stop every individual and have him carefully examined before he is allowed

to cross our line. But we have also to take into consideration the necessities of travel, the convenience of travellers and people who are passing across; and we have tried as much as possible to harmonize the safety of the people with the convenience of travellers. That has been our sole aim in the administration of this work. I can assure my hon. friends opposite that not only myself but my officers have in every case dispensed with the services of physicians just, as soon as it seemed to be possible in the interest of the locality that we were watching.

Then we ought to have a return showing the number of cases that were either quarantined or turned back at the line. Because if the aim of the minister be to keep out disease-and he has read the number of eases in Ohio, and the number in Michigan, the number in Minnesota-I would like to ask him how it is that there is no quarantine officer stationed at Sarnia, none stationed at Windsor, none stationed at Niagara Falls, while there are officers stationed at small places where not one passenger crosses for every hundred passing at these places that I have named. Now, if there is danger of disease being imported, it will be greater according to the increased number of people who come across, and yet where the people cross iu the largest numbers we have no medical health officers stationed and no work being done. Does it not appear on the face of it to be a burlesque ? The minister says he has urgent demands from the people that this should be done.
I have no doubt of that, the desire of the people is to prevent the importation of disease. But what we complain of is that when we are paying money for this purpose we do not get beneficial results from it. We do not complain of the expense, if disease was kept out of the country, but we know for a fact that from time time it is allowed to come in by the officers who are paid the people's money to keep it out, and then the municipalities are put to great expense to stamp it out. Take the case I referred to, twenty or twenty-five cases of small-pox developing from that one case. Yet that case crossed from Michigan, the officer failed to detect it, and it is only discovered by medical men in the locality away in in the interior of the country, more than a couple of hundred miles from the frontier. Yet that patient says he was infected when he came from Dakota, the disease was out on him when he crossed' the line, and it was then that he should have been inspected by a medical man. Take the immigration department as well. The minister says that trachoma is not a quarantinable disease. We have been told from time to time by the Minister of Agriculture, iu whose department immigration is maintained
Immigration is under the Minister of the Interior.

The Minister of Agriculture appoints the quarantine officials. Now, would you not think it natural that a quarantine officer who inspects incoming immigrants would report to the immigration officer the^ number of those immigrants who were infected with trachoma and some of those diseases that are contagious ? [DOT]These cases are allowed to come in iu hundreds, whereas on the American side they are all turned back, as I am informed. I saw a report from an American inspector, who said that a very large number were refused admittance to the United States on account of disease, and were allowed to come in and roam through Canada as they liked. Now, when we are paying money for this purpose we complain that not enough care is exercised to prevent the importation of disease. If these medical men were doing their duty, if the government were compelling them to do it in such a way as to satisfy the people that disease could not be imported unless in exceptional circumstances, for instance, where the infection had occurred but the disease had not developed-I say unless a disease was imported under these conditions, it ought to be prevented. It is because It is not ascertained, because it is not prevented, and because we find it is imported notwithstanding this large amount of money paid out, that we object to the working of the system and ask for a better system. On the other hand, there is no medical mau in the world but will tell you how utterly impossible it is to go to a boat with 400 passengers and inspect them as they are rushing off the gangways as these have done. It is no use sending a medical man on board a boat after it has entered the port and expect him to make an inspection under these circumstances. It may sometimes take place, but I have seen over and over again that these passengers come off in dozens and hundreds, and no medical man in the world could examine them so as to know whether many of them were infected. It is because the department is playing this farce of a quarantine that we object to paying out money without getting the results to which we are entitled.
Would the hon. gentleman who has just spoken tell us when it was these men were allowed to come into Canada over the American boundary ?
They came in both in summer and winter. One came in about four months ago, and the other two years ago, the last two that came under my notice.
Was it before or after the regulation was made ?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: After the regulation was made, and during the time these men were earning the salary that Is paid them.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he knows to what stage small-pox had developed In the case to which he referred that came across the boundary ?

I told the Minister of Agriculture that my information from the patient himself was that the small-pox was developed to the full extent at the time he came across the border, and during all the time he was on the train. He came through Minnesota into Canada.

No doubt the hon. gentleman knows very Well that in some cases of small-pox you might have a full development, and yet it would not be apparent enough for any medical man to detect unless he made a very accurate examination to tell whether it was small-pox or not.

I admit that to be a fact, but what I say is that this man had the pustules developed over his face, head and hands and those portions of his body that were plainly visible to inspection in the event of any medical health officer having inspected him.
Could the hon. gentleman tell me where the man came from in the United States ?
I think he came from Dakota.	v
By what route ?
I cannot tell as I did not inquire.

It is quite true that we have not got an officer at every route coming in. It is possible at any time that a case may come across from the United States where there is no officer. Until we have an officer at every route we cannot absolutely protect the frontier. The hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) is complaining that we are spending too much money and he says that we ought to reduce our expenditure in this respect.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Because it is useless.

Then, I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) to say that we ought not to protect tlie frontier and that we ought not to have these officers along the frontier to prevent the introduction of this disease ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman ought to have officers at the important points such as Niagara Falls, Kingston, Sarnia and at points where railways and ferries cross. In place of that the hon. gentleman has officers away up at Beaver Mills, Mine Centre. Bruce Mines. Chippewa. Owen Sound. Tliessalon and all those places where
there is not one person crossing for every thousand that crosses at the points I have named. Therefore I say it is a fraud and a farce to throw away the money of the country in the way it has been done. We have no protection at all. It is simply giving a sop to some of the hon. gentleman's Political supporters who claim that a certain doctor is a good political agent like the hon. gentleman w!ho sits beside him (Mr. Dyment) w'ho has one at Beaver Mills, and one at Mine Centre drawing $100 a month and who are, no doubt, political canvassers in that large country. There is not one person who goes into those parts of the country for every 10,000 who cross at Niagara Falls, or Sarnia, where there is no officer to protect the frontier. What a farce it is !

My hon. friend says perfectly truly that there are thousands crossing at Niagara halls and Sarnia for every one crossing at other places, but at the same time my hon. friend chooses for his own purposes to ignore absolutely that in the State of New York and around Detroit and opposite Sarnia and Windsor there are complete and effective organizations on the part of the United States to control and manage that disease.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then why appoint a man at Chippewa.
There was for a short time a flurry of excitement. for which reason an officer was appointed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why at Cornwall ?

In the same way there was a little flurry of excitement and when there is a flurry of excitement it is necessary to allay public alarm and meet the views of the authorities. In the case of Michigan and Minnesota, from which states people come to Thes-snlon, Bruce Mines and Beaver Mills, there is no effective control of the disease by the United States authorities and therefore we have to take precautions that we do not have to take in watching the passage of people from places like the State of New York and in the neighbourhood of Niagara and Buffalo where such a complete control is exercised as it is also exercised in the neighbourhood of Detroit.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why are Windsor and Sarnia neglected ?
Because opposite Windsor and Sarnia there is a complete organization.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
In Michigan ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE Yes, in that part of Michigan there is an organization. But in the northern lumber woods of Michigan from which people come to Bruce Mines and Tliessalon there is no

organization. There is no use in the hon. gentleman undertaking to misrepresent the state of affairs.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Auditor General's Report represents it fairly and I take my information from it.
I am not denying one fact in connection with the Auditor General's Report, but I am stating the grounds upon which we make these appointments.
How do these people get to Bruce Mines without going to the Soo where the hon. minister has a medical officer ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There are two of them at the Soo.
What is the necessity of having one at Bruce Mines ?
I am informed that there are vessels that come across from Michigan to Bruce Mines which do not go to the Soo at all.
Boats on their up trip go to the Soo and then cross over to Mackinaw and then cross to Bruce Mines which is the first port they call at on the Canadian side after leaving Michigan.
What line of boats ?
The Northern Navigation Company's boats sailing from Colling-wood.

The remarks made by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) may apply to the country which he represents west of Port Arthur but they do not apply to the portion of country from [DOT]which I come. Why should there be a medical officer appointed at Owen Sound unless for political purposes ? The railways running into Owen Sound do not come from any American port ? It is no part of the duty of the medical officer to attend the incoming trains and pass the people who get off those trains. The only duty he can perform is to visit the boats which may touch at American ports. Now, there are two lines of boats that run to Owen Sound- the Northern Navigation Co. and the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers. You have an officer at Fort William, one at Port Arthur and one at the Soo, and there is no necessity for one at Owen Sound. The boats only touch at the Soo, Port Aruur and Owen Sound. They do not go to Mackinaw or any other port. The only line of boats to which this may apply is the one to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Dyment) has referred, the Mackinaw excursion boats. If it is necessary to have an officer at Owen Sound then is it not equally

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
necessary to have one at Collingwood ? Collingwood has no medical officer, nor Midland, nor any of those points, where those boats touch. There is no doubt this appointment in Owen Sound is purely a political one. and if all the officers are appointed with the same amount of wisdom as the one appointed at Owen Sound I think the money of the country is simply being wasted in this service. I would like to ask the hon. minister if he would kindly bring down one of those monthly reports ?
The MINISTER, OF AGRICULTURE. I have not one under my hand at present, but I will bring one down.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has in the main estimates an item, No. 5Sr:
Salaries and contingencies of organized districts and public health in other districts, $170,222.
That he is asking for this year. When that item comes up, I hope the hon. gentleman will have the monthly reports of all these officers and be able to give us full information. He asked for $110,000 last year, and now toe comes down with a supplementary estimate of $60,000 making the expenditure $170,000 for the present year. We have had a very large amount of this money wasted and I hope the bon. gentleman will be prepared, if we allow this item to go through, to bring down the information when the main estimate is taken up. We must have the names of the men and the work they do.
I have given the names.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes, but we want the monthly reports of the work they do, so that we may know if they are doing something for their money.

The minister should carry out the policy he advocated when he was in opposition, and that is that these physicians who receive $100 per month should not be allowed to compete in active practice with other medical men in the locality. That was the principle that the Conservative government went on, and even the present government has appointed a physician in Kingston and prevented him to do private practice. I would like the minister to give me an assurance that these men will not be allowed to continue in active practice, because in addition to its being unfair to other doctors, they may be absent attending patients when these vessels and trains arrive and so neglect their duty to the Dominion. In my constituency there is a boat crossing every day bringing carloads of immigrants, and there is no one to inspect them. Indeed it would be impossible to inspect them here as elsewhere, because the moment the boat arrives they are put upon the waiting train and started off for their destination. But the strange

thing about this whole thing is that while throughout all Ontario, from Glengarry to Port Arthur, we spent $9,677 on this service, $8,166, or nearly the whole of it, was spent in the constituency of Algoma. We need not wonder at the anxiety of the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Dyment). who sits behind the minister, trying to get this item through.

When we realize the good that may be done by this service, we should not stop to consider the expense of it. I do not know to what extent this service has been abused for political purposes, but I can easily conceive that even under the most careful scrutiny of a medical man, a case of the disease may come into Canada. If the appointees of this government do not scrutinize the ports of entry very closely, their services had better be dispensed with, because in order to perform their duty with any measure of success they must exercise the greatest care. The explanation of the minister as to the methods employed by these medical officers have not been satisfactory to me. We are not instructed as to whether the trains are held up until the medical officer makes his inspection, and we know that if a train is allowed to stop at a station people get on and get off, and those affected with smallpox may not come under the scrutiny of the medical officer at all. If a case of smallpox is well developed any medical officer can easily detect it, and in that way the service is important and useful, but even under the closest scrutiny certain types of the disease may escape detection. We know that in the frontier towns of the United States there have been numerous cases of small-pox, and if I were assured that these medical officers carefully discharged their duties, I would be more reconciled to this vote. I would not attempt to discourage the service, but X fear there is ground for the complaints made by hon. members on this side of the House that the service has been abused for political purposes.

It appears to me that the government is taking great care of the United States people, while they are neglecting their own people in the interior of the country. From Cornwall to Uake Superior there are large stretches of water which make it difficult for disease to come into Canada in that territory, and yet all this money is spent there while from Cornwall to the Ste. Croix river, where the- international boundary is on land, the government take no precautions at all. In the county of Dorchester which I have the honour to represent, there were some cases of small-pox last year, and the municipal council passed a resolution preventing people from going within four miles of where the disease existed. This shows what precautions we take in the county of Dorchester, but it would appear that the Min158
ister of Agriculture thinks that it is only necessary to protect the constituency of Algoma, in which he has spent all this money. At St. Johns, Quebec, where many railroads centre and where the people from Montreal and Quebec cross to the New England States, and vice versa, there is no precaution taken, whatever, by the government. Can the minister explain that '?

I can explain that very easily. In the first place we are not taking care of the people of the United States, but we are trying to protect the people of Canada by keeping out disease which may come from the United States. The Dominion government has nothing to do with the interior of the country, because that is looked after by the provincial or local health authorities, and our duty is only to protect the frontier. There has been no physician appointed at St. John, Quebec. The reason is that the provincial health authorities have expressed to us their entire satisfaction with the condition of affairs, saying that they have no fear of the introduction of disease along the Quebec frontier. We do not know of any disease in the state of New Hampshire or the state of New York, the state health authorities having it so well under control. We do not appoint these officers anywhere unless there appears to be danger; we do not appoint them unless the local or provincial health authorities have made a demand for their appointment; and we appoint them only after an examination by the medical officers of the department to assure themselves that the fear on the part of our own people seems to be reasonably well founded. The hon. member for South Grenville (Mr. Reid) has asked me to assure him that we will not allow physicians occupying this position to carry on their own practice. I do not think I can give him that assurance. If I were to do so, it would be with the utmost difficulty that I could get medical men to accept these positions. The salary given would be no temptation to them. Even as it is, we have great difficulty in many places in getting doctors. If we were to forbid them engaging in any private practice, we would cut out all the physicians along the frontier who are now in office, because they could not afford to give up their ordinary practice for the purpose of getting a temporary appointment lasting perhaps a few months, though in some instances a year, at $100 a month. The hon. gentleman is a physician, and he knows perfectly well that that salary would not tempt any physician of decent standing to give up his practice and take such an appointment. We would have to fall back entirely upon young physicians who have just passed their examinations. The result would be that we could not get officers to do the work. Therefore, I cannot give the assurance the hon. gentleman desires. But while these officers are allowed to carry on



their private practice, they are not allowed to do it in such a way as to interfere with their duties as officers of the department.
Do not let my hon. friend misunderstand me. There is no one of these appointments for the year.
But some of them are engaged for twelve months.
They might be dismissed at any time.
If it is understood that they are for the year ?
That is not understood in any case.
Is the hon. gentleman not asking a grant for the whole year ?

I am not asking a grant to pay for the whole yeai\ I am basing my estimates on the expenditures of the last two years; but there are comparatively few of these officers who were on for the whole year. I cannot say how many, but certainly less than half. The amount I am asking would not pay them the whole year round.

I admit that. For instance, this man at Beaver Mills is in active practice. I ask that he and the man at Mine Centre and the man at Sault Ste. Marie be asked to discontinue active practice, or else that the appointments be given to physicians who will take them and give up active practice. I think that is not unfair. I only ask that in places where you are paying the officers for twelve months service, and I ask it in justice to the other physicians of the different localities.

The hon. gentleman has particularly mentioned the doctor of Sault Ste. Marie. I am told that he was wanted for that position by almost everybody in Sault Ste. Marie, irrespective of politics. His practice is worth to him at least $5,000 Hen. Mr. FISHER.
a year, if he devoted all his time to it, so that it could hardly be expected that he would give that up to accept $100 a month for an indefinite period, or even for a full year.

The hon. gentleman says I mentioned Sault Ste. Marie in particular. He knows I did not. I mentioned every case where a physician is appointed for twelve months. The hon. gentleman knows that the first place I referred to was Beaver Mills. Perhaps he can tell us whether there is another physician at that point ?
I do not think there is.

Then, why not let another physician go in there and do this work 1 I would say the same of Mine Centre. That rule has been followed on both sides of the House, and I think it is only just to the physicians practising in the different localities. If this man at Sault Ste. Marie does not wish to give up his practice, there are just as good men to do the work. Will the hon. member say that if this man is doing a practice of $5,000 a year, he can attend to this work every day ? It would be impossible for him to attend every train and every boat at Sault Ste. Marie. I appeal to the minister to protect the physicians practising in these different localities. He knows that if he sends out and asks for applications for these positions, he will have a thousand applications inside of two weeks from men who will accept them. I appeal on behalf of the interest of these physicians practising in these localities, that the department should insist on these men discontinuing their active practice or else give up their government appointment.

The hon. gentleman would be quite right if this were a permanent position, but it would be difficult to get any good men to settle down in these places on a monthly salary with the possibility of their service's being discontinued at any moment. The hon. gentleman says that the practice lie lays down is well understood. I was not aware of that. I can refer him to the port of Halifax where the port physician, under one of my predecessors, carried on his regular practice and drew a salary from the government besides.
What was his salary ?

$1,800 per year.
air. REID (Grenville). When the hon. gentleman states that he could not get a physician to go out to Beaver Mills with the possibility of being employed only a few months in the year, let me tell him that if he will leave the matter to me, I will get a physician

 .
Would you go V
No, but I would get a better man than myself to take the position at $100 per month with the risk of being only employed some months.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman explain what Dr. B.' Gibson's duties are and how he attends to them ?

He meets all the trains coming from Michigan. They of course have regular stated times for coming in, within a few minutes every day, and he can arrange his engagements so as to be at the stations when they come.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What about the boats, are they included ?
One year there was an assistant to Mr. Gibson to meet the boats. I do not know whether there is one this year. This man spends practically the "whole of his time at the docks looking after the boats.
I would ask the hon. minister whether these inspectors stop people who are infected with trachoma and favus ?
No, they are not quarantined.

I think that it is time the government took an active part in preventing people infected with these diseases from entering this country. They are not adi mitted to the United States. Forty per cent of the immigrants at Winnipeg, en route to the United States who applied to the American Board of Inspection of the United States were rejected. Two thousand of them at Montreal, destined for the United States were rejected last year who applied for permits to go into the United States were also rejected. Such people are undesirable citizens and we should not allow them to be dumped on us. If they are not fit to be citizens of the United States, they should not be allowed to remain in this country, but be deported altogether. I presume, however, that this discussion will come up better on the item of immigration and I hope that the Minister of the Interior will be here soon.

I notice an item of $720 for an inspector at Fort William, and the same amount for an inspector at Port Arthur. These two towns are within a mile or two of each other and are connected by a street railway system. Furthermore, on the line of railway which runs through that section, there is not a train which does not touch both towrns. Nor is there a boat that touches Port Arthur which does not go to Fort William as well. Why is it necessary to keep an inspector at each of those places?

There are boats from the United States, some of which go to Port Arthur and others 158J
to Fort William, and each of these ports has to be guarded. There is a large number of people continually crossing from the lumber woods on the south shore to the lake and going to work in the lumber woods on the north shore. In the lumber woods in Michig'an and the south shore of Lake Superior, there is a considerable amount of this disease, and it is desirous to guard against it being brought into our country.
Does the hon. minister say that there is a line of vessels which runs to Port Arthur and does not call at Fort William ?
A number of vessels go to Fort William which do not go to Port Arthur.

It is evident that smallpox is imported from northern Michigan into Ontario. In the lumber woods of Ontario it has broken out from time to time. Last year away around Sudbury it prevailed most of the year. Almost every month of the year it can be found there. The fact that it is imported from Michigan to that extent shows how imperfectly this work is done. We are not complaining of the act in trying to keep up the quarantine, but we complain about paying out money and getting no benefit in return. If it were necessary to cite any particular case to show that the work is not properly done, the one cited by the hon. member for Algoma might be mentioned. You employ a man by the year at $100 per month, and according to the hon. member for Algoma he has a practice which gives him $5,000 per year. Well, everybody knows that a man with a practice of that kind has all his time taken up and cannot possibly attend to government business. He may be detained in a house hours at a time and therefore cannot possibly fulfil his duty as quarantine officer.

I can assure the hon. member for East Grey that the doctor I referred to does attend to his duty, and if he were to leave it, I firmly believe, protest would come from members of his own party rather than friends of my own. His practice is altogether a city practice, and ns these trains come in with great regularity, it is quite possible for him to make arrangements to meet those trains and then attend to his other cases. I know that he has the confidence of the whole town of Sault St. Marie, irrespective of politics. I am sure that my Conservative friends there would be the first to ask to have him retained if the proposal were made to dispense with his services.

I am not saying a word about the professional ability of the medical man. He may be the best in the world, or he may be the worst. But to say that the medical man who is employed to the

extent spoken of in every day practice can be available to attend trains when they arrive, is to say what to medical men will be manifestly absurd. You do not have sickness when you can attend to it most conveniently; it comes every day and every hour. The medical man may be detained for hours at a time, and he cannot leave a patient just when he pleases.
The MINISTER OB' AGRICULTURE. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) says he has no objection to the work if it is done effectively, but that he knows that it is not done effectively. I will not give him any statement of mine, but I may give him a few facts upon which he can form his own opinion. The Ontario provincial authorities have to pay the expense where there are outbreaks of small-pox in the unorganized districts, but the municipal authorities have to pay the expenses of an outbreak in an organized municipality. These people take the ground, and I believe properly, that where they can prove that an outbreak of disease is the result of importation of the disease from across the line, they can make us pay for it. In the last three years, during which this work has been carried on, a demand has been made upon this government for the payment of these expenses in only two cases where those mjaking the demand could establish their complaint. In one case the outbreak was due to a man who crossed the ice on foot above Sault Ste. Marie. It was shown that he had small-pox upon him when he crossed. He escaped the _ vigilance of our officers, but in a way against which it would be practically impossible, in my opinion, to guard. In the other case, a passenger came across at Sault Ste. Marie and got as far as Sudbury. He concealed himself on the train and was not seen until the conductor came across him on the train at Sudbury. In these two cases we had to pay the expenses. If there had been other cases to which the hon. gentleman referred, I have no doubt but that the provincial authorities and the municipal authorities, who are in charge of these matters, would have placed the responsibility upon my department and demanded payment. This rule is true for Manitoba, the Territories, British Columbia and every other province. Yet, these two cases are the only two in which it has been shown that the affected people came from across the line and escaped the vigilance of our officers.

I have given the hon. minister two cases, and in both these cases the municipalities paid the cost of stamping it out.
The MINISTER OB' AGRICULTURE. I do not think they could make a good case.

It is probable that some of these parties do not know that the Do-Mr. SPROULE.
minion can be held responsible. Or, it may be, that they do not care to take the trouble to collect the money. Rather than engage in a troublesome and expensive lawsuit the municipality bears the expense.
The MINISTER OB' AGRICULTURE. There is no lawsuit about it.

I think I remember a case that was presented from Winnipeg a few years ago. And, after a great deal of work, the result was that the city got nothing, and the cost, borne by the city, amounted to about $2,000.

I do not know the case to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) refers. But I believe there was a case in which the government did pay. There was no law case about it. The representations were made to the government, the case was made out and the government paid.

In the case I speak of the government refused to pay. I remember the case, because I was one who went to the government on behalf of the city of Winnipeg, and the government declined to be held responsible, because the immigrants were inspected by their quarantine officer, though the disease developed among them in Winnipeg.

Will the hon. minister say how much the supervision of these eases cost the department ?
The MINISTER OB' AGRICULTURE. I am informed that the cost amounted to about $700 or $750. I have not-the exact figures.

The hon. minister has not made it clear on what principle he bases the payment to these officers who keep the small-pox; from coming in from Michigan. It appears that we have medical officers in Port Arthur and Port William, about a mile apart, and others at various points along the North Shore, while there are none at Sarnia and Windsor. The hon. minister says that the authorities in Detroit are well organized. But surely there are other people coming into Sarnia and Windsor besides those coming from Detroit. Men from all parts of the state of Michigan may come in at Sarnia or Windsor just as they come across at Sault Ste. Marie.
The MINISTER OB' AGRICULTURE. At Detroit there is a well organized system, but for the northern part of Michigan, where the lumber camps are, there is not.
Why cannot these people from northern Michigan come across at Windsor or Sarnia ?
They would be stopped by the officials in the southern part of Michigan.
Are there people engaged In watching the people of the northern part of Michigan to prevent them from coming into Canada ?
The organization is of a municipal character. They would not allow the people with the disease upon them to enter their municipality.
But how is that carried out ? They cannot stop ,a train coming in from the northern part of Michigan and inspect it.
I cannot say what precautions they take, but the report is that they watch the disease, and that report is of such a character as to satisfy my principal officer that there is no danger there.

I have been wondering if this is not a provincial matter. The provincial government have their board of health and they have a provincial health officer. Why does the Dominion government look after these interior ports ?
What interior ports ?

Owen Sound and others in the province' of Ontario. I can understand the quarantining of ports into which immigrants come from European countries, but I do not see why this other work in the interior is not done by the provincial authorities.

That question was submitted to the Department of Justice before we undertook this work, and we were told that we are responsible for the frontier between the United States and Canada just as much as we are for the sea-board.
Does this government have anything to do with supplying of the vaccine ? Have they got a farm where they develop vaccine ?

We have no vaccine farm. There has been some discussion as to the advisability of the government undertaking the manufacture of vaccine, but we have not yet undertaken it.
Department of Marine and Fisheries-contingencies-further amount required, $1,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is this for ?

At the end of the fiscal year, 1902, the sum of $878 was carried forward and paid out of the appropriation for the current year. In order to square up the accounts this amount is required to be voted.
Ocean and river service-further amount required for Dominion steamers, $30,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman explain that ?

The appropriation for 1902-3 was 5225,000. That includes the cost of sending a crew to Scotland to bring out the new steamer and repairing damage done to the ' Lady Laurier ' by heavy storm on the ocean. The appropriation was found inadequate, owing to the large expenditure in connection with the Dominion steamers running between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. The amount required for the maintenance of all the steamers was $240,569, so that the amount voted was insufficient. The expenditure for the current year is estimated to be $255,000 in all, this will make an extra amount of $5,000 over the estimate of the fiscal year 1903-4. Owing to the damage done to the steamers while caught in the ice during the winter, both steamers have been put on the marine slip. The ' Minto ' had to have her propeller blades renewed, and the ' Stanley ' had also to be placed on the slip to be partially rerivetted on the bottom. This work will necessitate a large expenditure, in addition to this the indentations will be taken out of the sides of the ' Stanley ' and intermediate frames put in to reinforce the plating.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not clearly understand why we have to pay this further amount of $25,000.
The amount voted was $225,000, instead of $255,000, which has been expended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Last year the minister said that $225,000 would be sufficient. What is wrong in his estimate ? Why this over expenditure ?
I did not make that estimate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister knows he is responsible for it. The statement was made last year that the sum which we voted would be sufficient to carry us through to the end of this current year. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could give us some details of the purposes for which this extra sum is required.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's predecessor asked us for an amount that he could run the business for. But there has been a change in the head of the department, and the hon. gentleman has probably been extravagant in spending this $30,000 more than was voted, and hence this ur-gehcy now. Had his predecessor remained in office, I do not think he would have required this extra amount.

I suppose if my predecessor had remained in office, he would still have required this vote. I entered the office on the llth of November, nearly at the end of
:035

the season of navigation, and I had to take tlie government steamers in the condition in which I found them. There were extensive repairs to be made, as I have explained. The ' Aberdeen,' for instance, had to be repaired and repairs to the extent of $8,304 were done.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Who did the repairs ?
The MINISTER OB' MARINE AND FISHERIES. They were mostly done on the ' Aberdeen ' by day labour.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where ?
In Quebec and Halifax. Then, there were very extensive repairs to the ' Minto ' and ' Stanley ' ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
What was the amount of each 1
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. $15,000 on the ' Stanley ' and $7,000 on the ' Minto.'

Were not these $15,000 of repairs	foreseen by	the department ?The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. They could not be foreseen.

Therefore, there must have been some accident.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. There was. Everybody is aware that during last winter the ' Minto ' and ' Stanley ' were caught in the ice and that the 1 Minto ' was disabled. W'e had to repair the ' Minto ' in order to put her into service again. We had also to repair the ' Stanley.'

Were these repairs made at Quebec ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. The ' Aberdeen ' was repaired at Quebec, the ' Minto ' at Pictou and Charlottetown and the ' Stanley ' at Charlottetown and Pictou during the fiscal year.

What firm carried on the repairs to the 'Minto' and 'Stanley'?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Bruce, Stewart & Co., of Charlottetown, made the repairs to the ' Stanley.' They are the only people able to do such work on the island.
Mr-. MONK. And who made the repairs at Pictou ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. J. & J. Yorston.

Were these repairs done by day's work or by contract ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. It is impossible to make a contract for repairs of this kind. We get our own officers to make an investigation and to specify what repairs are necessary, Hon. Mr. FISHER.	,
but it is almost impossible to say in advance by 25, 30, or 50 per cent what will really be required to be done. But, they are always within the estimate and we have very good officers in that part of the maritime provinces.

Still, in the case of repairs amounting to $0,000 and still more in the case of repairs amounting to $15,000 I could scarcely conceive that it is impossible that these repairs can be carried on by contract as they always are in Montreal by steamers that have to be repaired there. At any rate it would be possible to have an estimate made beforehand and to be able to show the committee whether the expense actually incurred tallies with the estimate. I would like to ask my kon. friend if these precautions were taken in these two cases, because, it seems to me, barring the case of accident, that this is a very large extra amount, $30,000 in a sum amounting to a little over $200,000. and I think we are entiitledi to the fullest information. It seems to me that the hon. minister might be able to state the reason of this rather extraordinary expenditure so that the committee will feel fully justified in voting this amount if these precautions have been observed.

All these precautions were taken. All these repairs were made within the estimate of our officer who examined the steamers before the repairs were made and examine them also while the work was going on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I shall not push my inquiries any further. It seems to me in a case of this kind it would be much simpler if the department had an estimate made before the work began with accounts of the work done and if all this were put in a tabulated statement and laid on the Table of the House an item such as this could be disposed of in two minutes without all these questions being asked and the business of the House could proceed.
I have no objection to doing that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am just mentioning this to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister stated that he got hold of these vessels in November and that he had to make extensive repairs to the steamer ' Aberdeen.'
That is one of them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much was spent on the ' Aberdeen ' ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much did Mr. F. X. Drolet, of Quebec, get out of it ?
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman, hut I will furnish the information.
speakername: Tlie MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: These repairs have been done and this $8,364 has been spent. To whom was it paid ?
We have to put the ' Aberdeen ' in commission early in the season to see to the lighthouses, buoys and so on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman took charge of that steamer on which he spent $8,304 his predecessor had spent $6,000 for repairs with one firm in Quebec.
That was in the year previous.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Certainly it was in the year previous. It appears here in the Auditor General's Report covering the period from July, 1901, to July, 1902.

There is nothing extraordinary iu that. The * Aberdeen ' does double service. She does service during the sum-, mer between Quebec and the maritime provinces and when navigation closes between Quebec and the maritime provinces she does winter service below Halifax and around the maritime provinces. Now and then that steamer has to be repaired. It is impossible for a steamer doing the heavy service she Is doing to continue without being repaired, as everybody knows that steamers engaged in ordinary passenger traffic are obliged to undergo repairs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not wonder at the over expenditure because Mr. F. X. Drolet, of Quebec, draws $6,633 for doing some repairs for this steamer and furnishing some supplies. Mr. Drolet supplied tubes, 104 pounds at 60 cents a pound and he charges 3 cents a pound for 5,930 pounds of iron when $1.S5 to $1.90 per 100 would be quite sufficient. He charges for labour on board the steamer 387J hours at fifty cents an hour, and from $3.50 to $5 a day for men to make repairs. That is the way the money is spent. Everything is charged double. Mr. Drolet drew $6,000 out of the money we voted last year, and I have no doubt that he is getting a large share of this $8,000 for doing this work for which $6,000 was paid a few' months before.

If there is anything wrong about these accounts it is very easy to have them scrutinized before the Committee of Public Accounts. Since last my estimates were up, I have made inquiries and I have ascertained from the accounts and from the explanation given by Mr. Gregory, our agent at Quebec, that there does not appear to be anything wrong. Mr. Gregory, who looks after these things, has been in the department for thirty-four years, under all governments, and up to the present time he has done nothing deserving of reprimand. The accounts of Mr. Drolet, or any body else can be examined before the Public Accounts Committee and can be justified to the last cent. Mr. Drolet is one of the best machinists in this country. He is the best machinist in Quebec, and these accounts have been verified by our officials from day to day. After we have taken all these precautions the department cannot be held responsible if there is anything wrong, and before any charge is made against the department, these accounts surely ought to be scrutinized before the Public Accounts Committee. Since the last discussion I have written Mr. Gregory to be ready at any time to come here with all the - facts connected with these repairs, and Mr. Gregory has sent to the department an explanation which seems to me perfectly satisfactory. But if lion, gentlemen are not satisfied, they can have an examination before the Public Accounts Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am satisfied that the accounts which will be brought down be- . fore the Public Accounts Committee are correct so far as making the calculation goes.
What I mean is that the amounts charged are reasonable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister is a business man and he ought to know that $5 a day is too much to pay for a man working on repairing a steamer.

I am enough of a business man to know that men are worth $5 a day when they are making certain repairs to machinery, and the work is done in a machine shop where steam plant is used as well as mechanical skill and labour. In the city of Montreal at the present time we are paying $4.50 per day to bricklayers, and you cannot compare the work of a bricklayer with the work of a mechanic who repairs very intricate and delicate machinery. I have had experience in Montreal for a long time not only for the public but in connection with enterprises with which I am connected, and I am well aware of what prices are paid. We must take into consideration the use of the expensive tools that these people have to use in this special work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I am satisfied there is not a machinist working in any machine shop in Montreal who gets any such wage as $4 or $4.50 per day. Let the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) tell the minister what he is paying for machinists in his locomotive works. The hardware men in this House who know their business have pointed out that everything that goes into the repair of these vessels is paid for at
