a higher price than you could buy them tor iu any country hardware store. You paid nearly double the usual price for zinc and magnolia metal, and you paid three dollars a hundred pounds for iron that any one can purchase to-day for $2.10 per 100 pounds, and the prices are higher to-day than they were last fall. No wonder the expenditure was exceeded last year, when such prices were paid.

The minister told us the other day that it was the policy of his department to purchase the supplies for the government steamers by tender. He also told us that last year the cost of these supplies was about $35,000, and I asked him if he would be good enough to furnish the Committee, at its next meeting, with information as to what proportion of that $35,000 was for purchases by tender and what proportion in the other way.
I will send over these papers to the hon. gentleman and he will see how the tenders were asked for and how they were dealt with.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is not what I want. I want to know what proportion of the $35,000 was for goods purchased by tender.

That would be very difficult to answer. If the hon. gentleman has any idea of business he will know that it would be impossible to give that statement without entering into a very extensive and intricate calculation. It must be remembered that these steamers do not get their supplies all at the same port. When the captains call for instructions they get their supplies in Halifax or St. John or Charlottetown, or wherever they may be. Sometimes they go to ports where we have no contracts and where we have no regular sources of supply, and they have to get necessary supplies at such places. It would be impossible to call for tenders in such cases, and we have to rely on the honesty and intelligence of our officers to purchase under the best conditions. The accounts are examined, and if the officers are satisfied that the prices are fair, the accounts are paid. If the prices are considered unfair, they are discussed and reduced. A business company would do the same thing. This system has been going on for the past fifty or sixty years, and it has not been changed by this government. I do not know where fault can be found. If some of the charges seem to be too high, it is not possible to obtain the explanation simply by reading the Auditor General's Report ; but if an explanation of any item is asked for before the Public Accounts Committee, it will be given.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What I say is that these supplies should be purchased by tender.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: They are.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister says that there is no difference between this side of the House and himself on that question. He says that the policy of his department is to purchase these supplies by tender. I find that $35,000 was spent for these supplies last year. Is it unreasonable for us to ask what proportion of these were purchased by tender, under the policy which the hon. gentleman says is adopted by his department ?

That information could be got, no doubt, but it would require a good deal of calculation and book-keeping to prepare the statement. I suppose that about seven-eighths of the amount are bought by tender. The rest were bought as the occasion may require. These accounts are all in the department, where they can be consulted, or they can be, produced in the Public Accounts Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Surely the hon. minister is not going to adopt the policy whenever a question is asked along this line, of referring us to the Public Accounts Committee. Does he state that [DOT] seven-eighths of the amount purchased last year was purchased by tender ?
That is the information the deputy minister gives.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This question of taking tenders for supplies for the government steamers has been discussed here several times. My hon. friend is new in the department and I am sure that with his experience and his information he would say that the taking of tenders for supplies would be of great use.
It is done.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. It is done in his department in the same way as in other departments ; letters are written to a few gentlemen, and they are asked to give prices-sometimes, not always. But we expect great reforms from my hon. friend he is greatly interested in the improvement of the St. Lawrence route; and I am sure that he would save at least thirty per cent in the cost of these supplies if he would adopt the simple method which is followed in other countries. If he will tell the committee this evening that next year he will positively give public notice that tenders will be received for supplies according to certain specifications, and that this notice will be given in the papers so that the public generally will have a chance to tender, I for my part will be ready to give him peace, and this amount will be voted without too much controversy.
I am ready to give the assurance that I will take the necessary precautions that supplies will be purchased at the lowest price In the market and in the best manner possible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But the hon. gentleman will not give the assurance that he will call for public tenders.

I will not, when it is not necessary and when I would have to spend twenty-five per cent or thirty per cent in advertising without getting any reduction in the price. For instance, you have to buy $1,000 or $2,000 worth of goods in a port like Charlottetown. If you advertised for tenders in the public press, you would have to publish your advertisement in all the papers. If I published it in only one paper, I suppose I would be reproached for that in the same way that I am for sending notices to one class of traders. In that case $500 or $000 would be spent perfectly uselessly, whereas, by sending circulars to first-class dealers and comparing their prices with the market prices, we get the supplies at the lowest possible cost. We are supposed to have competent and honest officers. Most of them belong to the party to which the hon. gentleman belongs, and we have sufficient confidence in them to keep them in office. We think they are doing their duty, and that is why we keep them. When a very large quantity of supplies is to be purchased, we call for public tenders; but when ordinary goods are required for a steamer, I do not think there is any necessity of calling for tenders.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am very much disappointed in the new Minister of Marine and Fisheries-bitterly disappointed. I do not think there is any question in what we are urging as to the efficiency of the officers. I have no doubt that they are good officers, whatever may be their party. My hon. friend will admit that to put an advertisement in a Montreal paper, a Quebec paper, and a couple of papers in the maritime provinces, stating that tenders for supplies according to specifications which would be furnished by the department, would be received, would not cost twenty-five per cent of what we would spend for these supplies. To call for tenders would, according to the hon. gentleman, cost from $20,000 or $25,000 for advertising. That is quite unreasonable. My hon. friend knows that that is the way we proceed in municipal affairs in Montreal, and the way steamship companies proceed all over the world. Why should not this government adopt that simple method 7 There is no reason, and I am very much disappointed with my hon. friend.
I am very sorry.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: On these tenders which the hon. gentleman has submitted to the committee there are one or two notes. At the bottom of one are these words : ' The names have been recommended by Senator Temple-man.' At the bottom of the other are these words : ' All names have been recommended by Colonel Tucker.' If tenders are asked for, the presumption would be that the lowest would be accepted, why then was it necessary that the names should be endorsed by the member representing the county 7
Before giving a contract to any firm, we inquire as to its responsibility, as any body would do in his private business. The lowest tenders were accepted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Were the supplies for the steamer ' Scout ' purchased by tender 7

The * Scout ' is a new steamer which is doing a new service and her supplies were furnished by people who had tendered. We asked for prices in the ordinary way without specifying to what steamer the goods should be delivered.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What service is the steamer ' Scout ' performing 7

Between Laeliine and Kingston, doing for the most part service for the Department in maintaining buoys in the St. Lawrence River and other work. The work will be increased by adding lighthouse attendance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I find in this list of tenders sent by the hon. minister to the hon. member for Peel, that very few are for supplies to Dominion steamers. They are mostly for lighthouse supplies. In the tenders for supplies for Dominion steamers to be delivered at St. .Tolin, I find that there are live tenders for five different supplies of groceries. The price for granulated sugar is 4} cents, whereas at Halifax the price tendered was 3'75 cents per pound. Yet at Quebec the hon. gentleman paid 54 cents per pound. Has the hou. gentleman the list for Quebec 7
I have not brought down all the lists. It would have been a very paying business, 'if when we wanted fifty pounds of sugar at Quebec, we sent to Halifax for it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman ought to know how much sugar is consumed on each steamer and if he can get it 3-75 cents per pound in Halifax he can buy a sufficient quantity there to supply each steamer. But here is the secret of the whole business. It is to be found in this endorsation by the

Liberal member. ' I recommend the acceptance of the above tenders. All the names are on the patronage list.' Thus three or four merchants, who are on the patronage list, are asked to tender, each for a different article, so that there is really no competition, yet according to these documents, although the hon. gentleman could have purchased all the sugar he required at Halifax at 34 cents per pound, he preferred paying five and a half cents per pound in Quebec. Is that the way the Richelieu Company do their business V
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I say that no business man would do business in that way. No wonder the hon. gentleman asked for an extra $55,000 to carry on the work.

I am a purchaser of sugar and know something about it. Sugar at 3'50 per lb, is Austrian sugar which comes to Halifax in bags and very inferior compared to what you get from our own refineries. People who want a good quality of sugar will not use it. It has been returned to me by some of my customers, and I was obliged to supply the best quality from the refineries in its place. There is as much difference in the quality of sugar as in the quality of tea.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Granulated sugar ?
We have inferior granulated sugar, and we have high-class granulated sugar.

Let us not assume from what the hon. minister has said that supplies are bought by public tender. As I understand it they are not so bought, it is merely a question of dividing the spoils and of the particular government supporter to whom this patronage shall be given. As the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Tucker) is present, I would ask him on what principle he advises the acceptance of the various tenders for supplies ? Are tenders publicly called for and does he recommend the lowest tenderer, or does he recommend the supporters of the government ?

I have not the faintest idea what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) is reading, except that it relates to certain tenders for supplies required by the government in the city of St. John. With regard to the amount to be paid with regard to the cost of those various articles, I know practically nothing. What I do know-and possibly this may be what the hon. gentleman requires-is that when I have been asked to recommend firms in our city of St. John to respond to the wishes of the department asking for these goods, I have recommended first class houses. Further than that, I do not think that I or any other hon. member of this House has the faintest Mr. TAYLOR.
right to deal with the almighty dollar-that is altogether foreign to our business. All I have to do is to give the names, and those names I am only too glad to give, selecting, as I do, the best men to carry out the wants and wishes of the government.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say that the same policy has been pursued for many years in the past ?
Twenty years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
This policy has been pursued for twenty years, and the hon. minister is pursuing the same policy now ? Let me read this document and perhaps the hon. minister will give attention to it and explain it :
The firms of E. B. Marvin & Co., and Peter McQuade & Son, were recommended to the department to invite tenders from for ship chandlery for the steamer ' Quadra.' The agent has been instructed several times to invite tenders for staple articles only. A tender form including a great many things that may or may not be required was given to each of those firms and they have tendered for nearly all the articles mentioned in the form. It is an old form used when we invited tenders publicly, and a tender for the lowest bulk stun was accepted, thus giving to one firm all the patronage.
Under the system that has been in force for the past three or four years-
That is, since hon. gentlemen opposite
came into power

-we have not invited tenders publicly.
The hon. gentleman tells this committee that the policy adopted thirty years ago is still in force. But this document that the hon. minister now submits to the committee with the old form of public tender attached shows that that form has been abolished and now a new condition of things prevails. Will the hon. gentleman now tell us that they are purchasing supplies in the same way as before ? The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has pointed out that we are only deceiving ourselves if we imagine that we are purchasing supplies by public tender. Would the bon. minister explain this new method of tender, and say if they have abolished altogether the public call for tenders ?
Did the document the hon. gentleman read say anything about a public form of tenders ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I will read it again :
A tender form including a great many things that may or may not be required was given to each of these firms and they have tendered for nearly all the articles mentioned in the form. It is an old form used when we invited tenders publicly, and a tender for the lowest bulk sum was accepted, thus giving to one firm all the patronage. Under the system that has been in force for the past three or four years we have not invited tenders publicly.
It seems to me that means a change.
.5045

The MINISTER OF MARINE ANI) FISHERIES. The matter is very easy to understand. This is for Victoria, B.C., I think. It may have been found easier, up to a certain time to ask for tenders publicly and to give the contract to only one person for all the goods in the complete list of articles to be furnished. Probably it has been found better to proceed in another way, that is, to buy from each firm the articles which were offered cheaper by that firm, and, in that way, to distribute the furnishing of these supplies to different traders. I know of these two forms of tender, and I know that sometimes although asking for tenders in that manner, the distribution is made to the different firms that have tendered the lowest for the different articles. Sometimes it is more advantageous to do it in that way, because you get the best articles at the lowest prices, and you are sure that tenderers do not control the situation. It might be that a tenderer having inside knowledge would know of certain articles mentioned in the list of which a very small quantity would be taken and these he would offer to furnish at almost nothing, knowing that his actual loss would be very small. Then, if you calculated the prices upon the whole list of articles, and gave the contract to the lowest tenderer, you might be obliged to pay a relatively high price for some staple article of which a considerable quantity is used and which you could have got at a lower price, though you would have low prices for articles of which little or none was used. I do not see much difference in the way of doing it. The principle is the same, except that it may be found more advantageous in certain cases to proceed by apportioning the articles among the different traders at the lowest price, than to give them to the same party.
Mr. OSLER, The fact is clear enough, there is no need of any further explanation from the minister, that originally, up to three or four years ago, tenders were invited publicly and now they are not. I read from a document the hon. gentleman sent over here, a report initialled by W. W. S :
Under the system that has heen in force for the past three or four years we have not invited tenders publicly.
There is the whole secret, and there is no use humbugging ourselves, and there is no use for the minister attempting to make us believe that the system of public tendering is in force now as it was.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I never said that public tenders were asked for, I said that circulars were sent to those who were on the list of the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I understood the minister to say that the system he is now following
is the same system that has been in force for the past twenty years.
That is the information that I have from my department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This document shows that statement is incorrect. I am reading from the document I have, this is a form of tender, and this is the information that is given by an official of the department. Don't let us make any mistake about this, or go away with an explanation which is no explanation at all. There can be only one reason, and that is that public tendering has been abandoned, and that tenders are only asked from those men who may be recommended by the member for the district. That is not public tendering, it is simply a division of the spoils.

It would be unwise for my hon. friend to go away humbugging himself. He should not do that, and he should not try to humbug anybody else. But he is conveying an impression now that there was a general system of public tendering in former years, and that that system has been changed. That is the impression that would be drawn from his remarks. Now, according to the document he has in his hands, he lias shown no foundation whatever for that impression.
I am speaking only from what I have before me.
Yes, and I have only the same thing.
Under the system that has been in force for the last three or {our years tenders are not invited publicly.
That refers to the port of Victoria, B.C.
Will the minister say that Victoria is the only port ?
No, 1 will not.
Will he say that system does not generally prevail ?
I will hear my hon. friend, then I will answer.

I am reading from this document which the minister has sent over here. I am speaking from knowledge of wihat has been the custom for the past twenty years, and with this document before me on which there is a direct statement by an official of the Crown that the system has been changed within the last three or four years, and that tenders are now asked privately and not publicly. Now, if Victoria is an exception, I would confine my remarks to Victoria only, and say that so far as Victoria is concerned, that so far

as tliis tender is concerned, and tliis particular case, it is not inviting public tenders, it is a mere distribution of patronage as the local member may recommend.

Then if my hon. friend's remarks are confined to Victoria, 1 cannot take much exception to them because the document seems to afford a foundation for his view. I asked the question whether the document had reference to public tenders, for this reason, that I was aware from general knowledge that the practice on the Atlantic coast has been for many years to invite tenders in the way described by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Now if any member would say that to his personal knowledge that is not correct, I would not assume the responsibility of denying it. But I am speaking from general information which I think is correct that as respects the Atlantic coast the method of buying supplies under the late government was precisely the same as under the present government. Therefore if the hon. gentleman wishes to point out that there has been a change in Victoria, that is a fair criticism, as the document shows, and I would leave the department to look into that. But I do not think that that change has taken place in the other ports of the Dominion. I know, at all events that the practice of the late government was to order supplies from their own friends on the eastern coast of the Dominion, and I always understood that the practice which now prevails as respects these ports of which I have the most knowledge, is exactly the same practice which has prevailed for many years. I am only taking exception to my hon. friend's remarks if they have a general application.

I think the Finance Minister will not tell me that this system ai>
plies only to Victoria, because the same form and the same suggestion are carried out here in asking recommedations, or purchasing supplies on the recommedation of some local member. Now the same recommendation is on each of these other forms of tender, the names are recommended by this member or by that member. So I say the inference is clear that the same form and the same system are in vogue in other ports as is clearly shown to be in vogue in Victoria; and I think, unless the minister can absolutely give a statement that Victoria is an exception, and that no change has been made in any other ports, the only inference we can draw is that there has been a general change.

The Minister of Finance a few evenings ago took issue witli me when I made the statement that the system of purchasing supplies had been changed in some places from the system followed by the former government.
I do not know that my hon. friend mentioned any particular place. He was dealing with the practice generally.

Here is an instance. I say that it occurs all along the St. Lawrence. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, if the statements of his crews are correct, must admit that they simply run in now and purchase their supplies at any port they wish, while under the late government they were purchased by tender.
There is no evidence of that.
Will the minister deny the fact ?
If they buy a pound of butter at the port where they stop, or a pound of sugar, of course I would not deny it.

The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he would kindly have a list of the names of the parties from whom he received tenders for supplies for the steamer ' Scout ' for the last year, for the information of the committee, because I am anxious to convince the hon. Minister of Finance that he is wrong in what he said in regard to that latter.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister admits that the department did not ask for tenders for the steamer ' Scout ' along the St. Lawrence. I am satisfied that I can produce evidence that previous to this government coming into power tenders were asked for.
I have told the committee that we do not ask for tenders for. particular steamers. We ask for tenders generally.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does my hon. friend persist in saying that for the incoming year he will not ask for tenders publicly ?
I cannot make any promise one way or the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: My hon. friend said a moment ago that he would not ask for tenders publicly. Does he still adhere to that determination ?

I never said anything of the sort. I said that we would proceed to the best of our judgment and ask for tenders for staple goods, for articles that can be furnished cheaper by getting prices fixed five or six months in advance at the different ports where supplies are required. I will not undertake to ask for tenders for articles that may be wanted in small quantities at periods we do not know in advance, and which may not be required at all. We will not ask for tenders for these articles, because it would not be in the public interest to do so, but, in future, if it is thought in the public interest to ask for tenders we will proceed to the best of our knowledge as we have been proceeding for the last number of years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell the committee that he will, at the beginning of each year, publicly advertise for tenders for supplies for the Dominion steamers ? Will he say that or will he not ? If he says he will not, I am perfectly satisfied.

If it is thought advantageous to do so we shall do so. But if we think that lay continuing in the way we are proceeding we will serve in a better manner the public interest, we will do it in that way, and leave the matter to be judged by the House and the people.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister has handed us a number of tenders which he claims are the lowest for the goods named in each. He must have received other tenders, and we would like to be furnished with those.
Yes, of course.

Oh, yes.

speechtext: A steamer, after receiving supplies at Halifax, leaves Halifax to supply the lighthouses, going from station to station, towards St. Paul Island, and then comes back and goes into the Bras d'Or lakes. That is often done, and it is impossible to stand upon tenders in all cases. There are circumstances under which it cannot be done.
